fields.title: The Key Teachings of Richard Baxter
fields.subtitle: An Ochorus companion to his life and teaching
fields.description: A concise, faithful guide to the pastoral heart of Richard Baxter — the saints' everlasting rest, the call to the unconverted, and the minister's charge to take heed to himself and to all the flock. Eighteen short chapters, each ending in questions and a prayer, written by Ochorus as a companion to Baxter's own public-domain works, which readers are warmly encouraged to go to directly.
fields.about_html:
This is a companion to Richard Baxter, not a book by him. Written by Ochorus, it renders the pastoral wisdom of the great Puritan of Kidderminster into eighteen short chapters in plain modern English.

Baxter wrote, by his own account, as a dying man to dying men, and the urgency never left him. Out of a lifetime of sickness and labour came books the church has never let go of: The Saints' Everlasting Rest, on the heaven the weary are travelling toward; A Call to the Unconverted, pressed on the careless with tears; and The Reformed Pastor, still the most searching book a minister can read about his own soul. This volume follows those themes and more — conversion, family religion, the crucifying of the world, counsel for the melancholy, peace among Christians — and ends each chapter, as Baxter would, in self-examination and prayer.

Baxter's own writings are in the public domain and freely available. Because his seventeenth-century English can be heavy going, this companion renders his thought into modern prose rather than quoting it, and names his works throughout so the reader may go to the source. Scripture is quoted from the Authorised (King James) Version.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. HEBREWS 4:9

There is a line about preaching that has been quoted in more sermons than almost any other in the English language. Its author said he preached as a man who could never be sure of preaching again, and as a dying man to dying men. Most people who repeat it could not tell you who said it. It was Richard Baxter, and it was not a rhetorical flourish. He wrote it as a plain description of his own circumstances. He was ill for most of his adult life, expected to die young for about fifty years, and buried the town he loved under an Act of Parliament. The urgency in his preaching was not manufactured. He genuinely did not expect to be there the following week.

A parish that changed

He is remembered for two things, and they belong together. The first is what happened at Kidderminster, a rough Worcestershire weaving town where he arrived in 1641 to find, by his own account, a parish largely ignorant of the gospel and given to drink. When he left, some twenty years later, the place had been transformed — so thoroughly that visitors came to see it, and the change was still spoken of a century afterwards. Whole streets sang psalms on their way home from work. He had to build galleries in the church five times. The second is how he did it, because the method was startlingly unromantic. He preached twice a week. And he set aside two full days every week to sit down with families in his parish, one household at a time, and go through the Christian faith with them personally — about fourteen families a week, some eight hundred families a year. He did it with his assistant, methodically, for years. That is the whole secret, and it is why his book on ministry has never gone out of print.

The other half of him

But Baxter is not merely the patron saint of diligent pastors, and a book that presented him that way would miss what he actually cared about. His most famous work is about heaven. The Saints’ Everlasting Rest was written in 1647, at thirty-one, while he lay gravely ill far from home and from his books, fully expecting to die. He wrote it, he said, for himself — a dying man’s meditations on where he was going. It became one of the best-loved books of its century, and it turned him from a country minister into a household name. The two halves explain each other. Baxter worked as he did because of where he believed people were going. He gave himself to catechising illiterate weavers because he thought each of them would exist for ever. Take away the rest and the labour makes no sense; take away the labour and the rest becomes sentiment.

How this book is arranged

Eighteen short chapters set out his teaching, beginning with the breadth of spirit that made him unusual, moving through his doctrine of heaven and the practice of heavenly meditation, then to conversion and justification, then to the pastoral work for which he is best known, then to the ordinary Christian disciplines — family religion, self-examination, the use of time — and finally to suffering, unity and dying well. Each chapter ends with application points and a prayer. Baxter would have approved and probably added more. He had an almost impatient conviction that truth which stops short of practice is worse than useless, and his great practical work — A Christian Directory — consists of nearly a million words of direct instruction on how to live. Read one chapter a day, or one a week. Stop at the application points. Pray the prayer, or better, pray your own. One note on the text. Baxter wrote a seventeenth-century English that many readers find heavy going. Throughout this book his teaching is summarised in modern prose rather than quoted, so that the argument comes through without the thicket. Readers who go on to the originals should be warned that the sentences are long and the pace is unhurried; that is the century, not the man.

One more thing must be said at the outset, and it is better said plainly. This is not a book of hero-worship, and Baxter is a particularly poor candidate for it. He was contentious. He spent an extraordinary proportion of his life in controversy — with bishops, with Independents, with Quakers, with Antinomians, with fellow Presbyterians — and he could not let an argument alone. He wrote around a hundred and forty books, many of them polemical, and he admitted late in life that he had written too much, too quickly, and too sharply. His doctrine of justification was widely judged to be a departure from the Reformed teaching of his own party, and the controversy over it outlived him by two centuries. Chapter six sets out what he held and where the objections lie. The reader should weigh it carefully rather than accept it on the strength of his other virtues. And his political judgment was, by his own reckoning, imperfect. He served as a chaplain in the parliamentary army and afterwards regretted much of what that side did. He helped bring about the Restoration and was then ejected by it. He was, as one modern historian has put it, a man who managed to fall out with almost every party in church and state, generally on principle and sometimes on temperament. Baxter knew this about himself. One of the most valuable things he ever wrote is a passage in his autobiography reviewing how his mind had changed with age: he had grown less confident of his own judgment, less impressed by his own learning, more charitable towards those who differed from him, and more convinced that the essentials of Christianity are fewer and plainer than controversialists suppose. It is a remarkable piece of self-knowledge from a man who had spent decades arguing. So the counsel of this book is the counsel of Scripture: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Where Baxter is faithful — and on the work of the ministry, the reality of heaven, the duty of personal instruction and the breadth of Christian charity, he is faithful indeed — receive it gladly. Where he presses beyond what is written, mark it, set it aside, and lose nothing.

A final word about the reader this book assumes. Baxter wrote for English weavers in a market town during a civil war, and for ministers scattered across a country tearing itself apart over church order. He is read now in places he never heard of, by Christians whose circumstances have nothing in common with his. The reason is that he wrote about what does not change: that people die, that they must be told the truth before they do, that ministers are answerable for those in their care, and that the ordinary household is where religion is either made real or quietly abandoned. Those matters are already waiting wherever this book is opened, and into whatever language it is carried.

fields.title: A Dying Man to Dying Men
fields.body_html:
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith. 2 TIMOTHY 4:7

A badly educated boy. Richard Baxter was born on the twelfth of November, 1615, at Rowton in Shropshire, in his maternal grandfather’s house. His parents were Richard and Beatrice Baxter; his father had gambled away much of the family’s small estate before his conversion, and money was tight. His education was, by his own bitter account, wretched. The village had a succession of teachers who were ignorant, drunk, or both. He never went to university — a fact that his opponents used against him all his life and that he never entirely got over. What he had instead was an appetite. He read everything he could obtain, taught himself theology, philosophy and medicine, and became one of the most learned men in England by sheer application. He was later described as the chief of the English Protestant schoolmen, which is a considerable thing to say of a man with no degree. His conversion came through books rather than preaching — a devotional volume that came into the house by accident, and afterwards the writings of the English Puritans. He dated his real awakening from that reading and never forgot it, which is one reason he spent the rest of his life pressing books into people’s hands.

Kidderminster. He was ordained deacon by the Bishop of Worcester in Advent 1638, kept a school at Dudley, and served briefly as curate at Bridgnorth. In 1641 he was invited to Kidderminster, a weaving town of some two thousand people in Worcestershire. The previous incumbent was reportedly incompetent and the parish neglected. Baxter was twenty-five. Then the country collapsed into civil war. He left the town, served as chaplain to the garrison at Coventry and afterwards to Colonel Whalley’s regiment in the New Model Army, where he spent his energies arguing against the sectarian opinions spreading among the soldiers. He came to regret a good deal about those years. In 1647 his health broke completely. He was taken in by friends at Rouse Lench, far from his library, and lay for months expecting to die.

It was there, with almost no books to consult, that he wrote the bulk of The Saints’ Everlasting Rest. He did not die. He returned to Kidderminster in 1647 as vicar, and stayed fourteen years.

What he did there. The ministry at Kidderminster became the most celebrated parish work in English history, and it is worth stating what it actually consisted of. He preached twice weekly, plainly, aiming at the conscience rather than at admiration. He and his assistant then devoted two whole days each week to personal instruction — summoning the families of the parish in turn, sitting down with each household, examining what they understood of the Christian faith, and teaching them individually. They worked through roughly fourteen families a week and covered the parish in a year. He organised the local ministers into an association that crossed the Presbyterian, Independent and Episcopalian divisions, so that discipline and catechising could be practised in common. He wrote continuously. He gave away a large part of a modest income. And the town changed. On his arrival, he reckoned, perhaps one family in a street showed any serious religion; when he left, there were streets where nearly every family did. He was careful to add that he claimed no credit for it and could name plenty of towns where better men had laboured and seen nothing.

Restoration and ejection. The monarchy was restored in 1660, and Baxter — who had worked for it — went to London as one of the king’s chaplains. He was offered the bishopric of Hereford and declined it. He asked for nothing except permission to return to Kidderminster, and was refused. At the Savoy Conference in 1661 he was the principal spokesman for the moderate Puritan party, and drew up a revised liturgy in a fortnight in the hope of a settlement broad enough to hold the moderates inside the national church. The hope was disappointed; there was no real appetite for compromise on the other side. The Act of Uniformity took effect on the twenty-fourth of August, 1662. Around two thousand ministers who could not subscribe were ejected from their livings on that day. Baxter, seeing what was coming, had already preached his farewell sermon in London the previous May. He was forty-six, and he never held a parish again.

Margaret. In September 1662, weeks after the ejection, he married Margaret Charlton. He was forty-seven and she was twenty-six, and the marriage astonished everyone, including a good many people who had assumed he would never marry at all. By every account it was extraordinarily happy. She was intelligent, decisive and devout, managed their affairs, and pressed him into ventures he would not have attempted alone. They lived through nineteen years of harassment, fines and forced removals together. She died in 1681, aged forty-five. Baxter, heartbroken, wrote an account of her life and character within weeks. It is one of the most affecting things in seventeenth-century English — a widower’s honest portrait of a woman he plainly considered his superior in several respects, published while the grief was raw.

Persecution. The years after 1662 were spent in and around London under a legal regime designed to make nonconformist ministry impossible. Baxter was harassed continually: forbidden to preach, fined, his goods distrained, his books seized, and moved from lodging to lodging. He was imprisoned briefly in 1669 for holding a conventicle. The serious blow came in 1685, when he was seventy and infirm. He was charged with sedition for supposed reflections on the bishops in his Paraphrase on the New Testament, and tried before Lord Chief Justice Jeffreys. The trial was a disgrace. Jeffreys abused him from the bench, called him an old rogue who had poisoned the world with his Kidderminster doctrine, and would not let his counsel speak. Baxter was fined a sum he could not pay and imprisoned for some twenty-one months in Southwark. He was released in 1686, and lived to see the Toleration Act of 1689 give nonconformists legal breathing room at last.

The end. His last years were spent in Charterhouse Square in London, still writing, still preaching when permitted, and in continual pain from ailments he had catalogued with a physician’s precision for half a century. He died on the eighth of December, 1691, aged seventy-six. Asked near the end how he was, he is said to have answered that he was almost well. He left around a hundred and forty published works, a parish that remembered him for generations, a manual of pastoral ministry that is still set for theological students, and a book about heaven written by a man who had spent fifty years expecting to arrive there shortly.

fields.title: A Mere Christian
fields.body_html:
Now this I say, that every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos …Is Christ divided? 1 CORINTHIANS 1:12–13

In 1680, worn down by forty years of being told which party he belonged to, Baxter wrote a sentence that has outlived nearly everything else he published. He said he was a Christian — a mere Christian — of no other religion, and that he would not be labelled by any narrower name. Nearly three centuries later C. S. Lewis borrowed the phrase for a book, and acknowledged where he had found it. Most people who use it now have no idea it began with a persecuted Puritan who could not get anybody to believe he was not a party man.

A man nobody could place

Baxter’s difficulty was that he genuinely did not fit. He was called a Presbyterian, and he was not one in any strict sense; he believed in a moderate episcopacy of the kind Archbishop Ussher had proposed. He was ejected as a Nonconformist, and he wanted to remain in the national church and worked hard to make that possible. He served the parliamentary cause and then laboured for the king’s restoration. He was attacked by strict Calvinists for softening the doctrine of the atonement, and by Arminians for holding to election, and by Antinomians for insisting on obedience, and by the Quakers for practically everything. He was, in other words, in trouble with everyone, and it was not accidental. He held that the essentials of Christianity are fewer and clearer than controversialists suppose, and that most of what divides believers belongs to a second rank of matters on which good men will differ until the Lord returns.

There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all. EPHESIANS 4:4–6

Baxter’s method was to ask what a person must believe and do to be saved, and to treat that as the ground of fellowship — refusing to make agreement on anything further a condition of receiving a brother.

Necessary things, doubtful things

The formula usually attached to his name is worth quoting accurately, and also worth attributing accurately, since he is regularly given credit for it: in necessary things unity, in doubtful things liberty, in all things charity. The saying did not originate with Baxter. It appears to come from a German Lutheran writer of the previous generation, Rupertus Meldenius, and has been misattributed to Augustine for centuries. What Baxter did was press it into English use and try to live by it, which is harder than coining it. The practical difficulty, as he knew perfectly well, is that everyone agrees with the formula and nobody agrees about which things go in which column. Baxter’s answer was to work from the apostolic summaries — the Creed, the Lord’s Prayer, the Ten Commandments — and to argue that what the church had required of converts in the first centuries was a reasonable measure of what was strictly necessary now.

Let us therefore, as many as be perfect, be thus minded: and if in any thing ye be otherwise minded, God shall reveal even this unto you. Nevertheless, whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule. PHILIPPIANS 3:15–16

That is Paul contemplating disagreement among mature believers, declining to force the issue, and telling them to get on together on the basis of what they already share.

Unity that was actually practised

Baxter’s irenicism was not merely a sentiment expressed in prefaces. At Kidderminster he organised the ministers of the county into an association that deliberately crossed the party lines — Presbyterians, Independents and Episcopalians agreeing to co-operate in discipline, catechising and mutual counsel, while leaving their disagreements unresolved. It worked, locally and for a time, and other counties copied it. That is more than most ecumenical schemes achieve, and it was achieved by a man who had strong opinions on every one of the questions being set aside.

Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. EPHESIANS 4:3

Note the verb. Not create the unity — keep it. It already exists; our task is to avoid destroying it.

The change he noticed in himself

The most valuable thing Baxter wrote on this subject is a passage of self-examination in his autobiography, in which he sets out how his mind had altered between youth and age. He had become, he said, less confident of his own judgment and more aware of how much he did not know. He was less impressed by clever men and more impressed by holy ones. He had come to think the differences between godly Christians smaller, and the difference between the godly and the ungodly larger, than he once supposed. He was slower to condemn, quicker to allow for honest error, and far more concerned with the few great truths than with the many disputed ones. It is a remarkable inventory from a man who had spent his working life in controversy, and it suggests that he learned something from all that arguing which the arguing itself could not teach him.

The limit

One caution, because breadth can become emptiness. Baxter was not indifferent to doctrine, and it would be a serious misunderstanding to enlist him for the view that beliefs do not much matter. He wrote enormous volumes defending positions he thought vital, and he went to prison rather than subscribe to terms he judged false. His charity was not vagueness; it was a considered judgment about which truths are load-bearing.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21

The test he leaves us is uncomfortably specific. Not do you approve of unity? — everyone does. But: name the group of Christians you find hardest to take seriously, and ask whether the thing dividing you belongs in the first column or the second.

A practical measure

The obvious objection to Baxter’s programme is that everyone claims to distinguish essentials from indifferent things, and no two people draw the line in the same place. He was aware of this, and he offered a working measure. His proposal was to look at what the church had actually required of converts in its earliest centuries. Before the great confessions, before the councils, before the divisions of the Reformation, a person was received on the basis of a short summary of faith, an undertaking of obedience, and baptism. From this he built his three-part standard: the Apostles’ Creed for what must be believed, the Ten Commandments for what must be obeyed, and the Lord’s Prayer for what must be desired. fields.body_html:
There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. HEBREWS 4:9

In 1647 Baxter was thirty-one years old and dying, or so everyone including himself believed. He had collapsed after two years as an army chaplain, was taken in by friends at a country house a long way from his library, and lay for months with almost no books to consult. He decided to spend what he assumed were his last months thinking about where he was going, and to write down what he thought. The result was The Saints’ Everlasting Rest, and it made him famous across England. He recovered, and lived another forty-four years. The book he wrote for his own deathbed was read at thousands of other people’s.

What rest means

Baxter began by defining the word, because it is easily sentimentalised. Rest is not idleness. The heavenly rest, as he expounded it, has two sides: a ceasing from what has wearied us, and an entering into the enjoyment of what we were made for. It is the end of labour and the beginning of possession.

Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord …that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them. REVELATION 14:13

The negative side is easy to state, and Baxter, in constant pain, stated it with feeling. There will be an end of sin — not merely of its guilt, which is already dealt with, but of its presence in us. An end of sorrow, of illness, of temptation, of persecution, of the fear of death, and of the sight of God’s church divided and harassed.

And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain. REVELATION 21:4

The positive side

But Baxter was impatient with a heaven described chiefly by what will be absent. The substance of the rest, he insisted, is God Himself. He set it out under three heads, corresponding to the three great faculties of the soul.

There will be perfect knowledge. Every believer who has ever struggled with the obscurity of Scripture, the silence of providence, or the reasons for his own suffering will have the answer — not as an argument, but by sight.

For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known. 1 CORINTHIANS 13:12

There will be perfect love. Baxter thought this the heart of it. The faculty we have used most poorly, spending it on things that could not repay it, will at last have an object worthy of the whole of it, and nothing in us will hold back. And there will be perfect joy, which follows from the other two, since joy is what happens when a soul knows and loves what deserves it.

Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore. PSALM 16:11

Rest with a Person

The organising idea is that heaven is not a place we enjoy but a Person we see.

Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is. 1 JOHN 3:2

Baxter drew out the sequence in that verse. Seeing produces likeness. The transformation we have been labouring at all our lives, with such partial success, will be accomplished instantly and completely by the sight of Christ. This is why he regarded a self-centred picture of heaven — reunion with the family, relief from trouble, the crown and the harp — as true but drastically inadequate. Those things are real. They are not the point. A believer whose hope of heaven could be satisfied by comfort and company has not yet understood what he is hoping for.

Why he wrote it

One more thing, and it explains the book’s tone. Baxter did not write The Saints’ Everlasting Rest as a work of speculative theology, and it contains very little curiosity about the mechanics of the next world. He wrote it as a practical remedy for a specific disease, which he considered nearly universal among Christians: that we believe in heaven and never think about it. The consequence, he argued, is a religion of dutiful misery. A believer who never contemplates his destination finds obedience burdensome, suffering intolerable, and death terrifying — not because his doctrine is wrong but because he has left the best part of it unused. The remedy is the subject of the next chapter.

There is a question worth carrying out of this one, and it is a fair test of whether the doctrine has become real. If heaven consisted of everything you currently associate with it — the absence of pain, the reunion, the rest — but God Himself were somehow not there, would you still want to go?

A rest we enter together

There is a dimension of the heavenly rest that Baxter felt more keenly than most writers on the subject, and it grew directly out of his circumstances. He spent his life watching the church of England tear itself apart. He was ejected by one side and distrusted by the other. He worked for forty years on schemes of reconciliation that came to nothing. Every party he tried to unite concluded that he belonged to the opposition. So when he wrote about heaven, the ending of division was not a minor item on the list. It was near the centre.

But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels, to the general assembly and church of the firstborn. HEBREWS 12:22–23

The general assembly. One gathering, undivided, containing all of them — the parties that would not sit at the same table, the men who wrote against each other, the traditions that anathematised one another. Baxter found this an extraordinary comfort, and also a rebuke. The rebuke is the useful part. If we shall spend eternity in the unbroken company of Christians we currently cannot be in a room with, then our present divisions are temporary in a way our theology admits and our behaviour denies.

That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us. JOHN 17:21

Baxter’s practical suggestion was to think about heaven whenever a church quarrel becomes bitter, and to ask how the matter will look from there. He found it shortened a good many disputes, though not, he admitted, all of his own.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Write down what you actually picture when you think of heaven. Notice how much of it is about you. 2. Take 1 John 3:2 and dwell on the sequence: seeing produces likeness. That is the mechanism of the change you have been labouring at. 3. Name the thing in your life that most needs the answer only heaven will give. Bring it to God as something to be waited for rather than solved. 4. Ask whether your religion has become dutiful. If so, consider whether you have left your destination unused. 5. Answer the question above honestly. If God were not there, would you still want it?

A PRAYER
Father, I believe in heaven and I almost never think about it, and my religion has grown heavy in consequence.
Forgive me for a hope so small that it could be satisfied by comfort and company. You are the rest. Not the absence of my troubles — Yourself.
Teach me what I am waiting for. Let the thought of seeing You do in me what my own labour has never managed.
And when the pain and the confusion and the divisions of Your church weigh on me, remind me that there remains a rest for Your people, and that I am on my way to it. Amen.

fields.title: Heavenly Contemplation
fields.body_html:
If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above …Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth. COLOSSIANS 3:1–2

The last part of The Saints’ Everlasting Rest is the part Baxter cared about most, and it is the reason the book was so widely used. Having spent several hundred pages describing heaven, he turns and asks a practical question: how does a Christian actually think about it? His answer is a discipline he called heavenly contemplation, and he set it out with the thoroughness of a man giving directions to a stranger in an unfamiliar town.

Why it must be deliberate

His starting observation is that this does not happen by itself. Believers assume that if they hold the doctrine, the comfort of it will be available when required — at a graveside, or in a crisis. Baxter’s experience was the reverse. The mind does not go to heaven of its own accord; it goes to whatever it has been trained on, which is generally money, work, grievances and the immediate future. A truth we have never dwelt on will not be there when we reach for it. So he prescribed a set exercise, at a set time, on purpose.

While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:18

Look is an active verb. The unseen does not force itself on our attention; it must be looked at.

The practicalities

Baxter was almost comically practical about the arrangements, and it is the most useful part of the whole treatment. Fix a time. He recommended daily if possible, and at least weekly for those who could not manage it — and he preferred a set hour, because occasional intentions evaporate. Sunday afternoons and evenings he thought particularly suitable. Choose the place. Somewhere quiet, free of interruption. Baxter himself liked to walk in the fields towards evening, and thought open air and solitude helped more than a closed room.

Come with the heart free. He advised choosing a time when the mind is not fresh from a quarrel or heavy with business, since a soul in that condition cannot lift. Take a text or a scene, rather than trying to think about heaven in general. Vagueness defeats meditation. Begin with a specific promise, a specific description in Revelation, a specific attribute of God.

Consideration, and then the affections

The structure of the exercise itself has two stages, and Baxter was insistent that most people stop after the first. The first stage is consideration — the deliberate work of the understanding. Turn the truth over. Ask what it means, what it implies, what it is worth. Compare heaven with what you are currently pursuing. Reason from what God has already done to what He has promised to do. The second stage is the engagement of the affections, and this is the point of the whole thing. Consideration is the bellows; the affections are the fire. Having thought about the truth, deliberately stir yourself to love it, long for it, hope in it, rejoice in it and grieve that you have neglected it.

Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. PSALM 73:25

Baxter observed that this is exactly what the psalmists do, and he made much of the practice of soliloquy — preaching to one’s own soul. The Psalms are full of it: Why art thou cast down, O my soul? A man may plead with himself as he would with another, and Baxter thought most Christians would be transformed if they addressed themselves half as directly as they address other people. The exercise ends in conversation with God — the meditation turning naturally into prayer, which is where it was always heading.

Two cautions

First, this can become a technique, and a technique can become a burden. Baxter was writing directions, not laying down a law, and a believer who ends up measuring his spirituality by how well the exercise went has misused it. Second — and this matters — some people cannot do this, and it is not their fault. Those weighed down by grief, exhaustion or the illness of mind Baxter called melancholy may find that sustained meditation makes them worse rather than better. He knew this and said so elsewhere, and we shall come to his counsel on it in a later chapter. Such a person should not conclude that heaven is closed to him because his mind will not settle.

The most useful thing in this chapter is also the smallest. Fix a time this week — twenty minutes will do — and take one promise about the world to come, and think about it until you feel something. That last clause is the whole discipline. Most of us stop at understanding, and wonder why the truth never warms us.

Using what you know

One of Baxter’s more unusual directions concerns the use of the imagination, and it needs stating carefully because it is easily misunderstood. He observed that the mind cannot conceive of what it has never encountered. We have no direct experience of heaven, and so an instruction to think about it frequently produces a blank. His remedy was to reason upward from things we do know. Take the deepest joy you have experienced — a reunion, a recovery, a burden lifted, the first hour of a holiday after a hard year — and then consider that this is a shadow cast by something greater, produced by a God who invented joy and has not exhausted His stock.

But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him. 1 CORINTHIANS 2:9

Baxter used the same method with relief from suffering. A person who has been in long pain knows something about what the cessation of pain will feel like, and may reason from the lesser to the greater. Two cautions, which he supplied himself. This is comparison, not construction. We are reasoning from Scripture’s own images to what they signify, not inventing a heaven to our own taste. The moment the exercise starts producing a place shaped by our preferences rather than by God’s presence, it has gone wrong. And it is a help for the affections, not a source of doctrine. Nothing learned by this method may be taught as fact. Scripture governs, and where it is silent we are content not to know.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Fix a specific time and place this week for one deliberate meditation on heaven. Twenty minutes is enough to begin. 2. Take one concrete promise rather than the subject in general. Vagueness defeats meditation. 3. Do not stop at understanding. Having thought, deliberately stir your affections — longing, joy, grief at your own neglect.

4. Try soliloquy. Address your own soul aloud as you would address a friend who needed persuading. 5. If your mind will not settle because of grief or exhaustion, do not force it or condemn yourself. Read chapter fifteen instead.

A PRAYER
Lord, my mind goes wherever it has been trained to go, and I have trained it on money, work and grievances.
Teach me to look at what is unseen. Not occasionally, when trouble drives me to it, but deliberately, at a set hour, as a discipline.
Take me past understanding into desire. Let me not merely think about the rest You have promised, but long for it.
And where my heart is too heavy to rise, be gentle with me, and lift it Yourself. Amen.

His remedy was to reason upward from things we do know. Take the deepest joy you have experienced — a reunion, a recovery, a burden lifted, the first hour of a holiday after a hard year — and then consider that this is a shadow cast by something greater, produced by a God who invented joy and has not exhausted His stock. But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him. 1 CORINTHIANS 2:9 Baxter used the same method with relief from suffering. A person who has been in long pain knows something about what the cessation of pain will feel like, and may reason from the lesser to the greater. Two cautions, which he supplied himself. This is comparison, not construction. We are reasoning from Scripture’s own images to what they signify, not inventing a heaven to our own taste. The moment the exercise starts producing a place shaped by our preferences rather than by God’s presence, it has gone wrong. And it is a help for the affections, not a source of doctrine. Fix a specific time and place this week for one deliberate meditation on heaven. Twenty minutes is enough to begin. 2. Take one concrete promise rather than the subject in general. Vagueness defeats meditation. 3. Do not stop at understanding. Having thought, deliberately stir your affections — longing, joy, grief at your own neglect. 4. Try soliloquy. Not occasionally, when trouble drives me to it, but deliberately, at a set hour, as a discipline. Take me past understanding into desire. Let me not merely think about the rest You have promised, but long for it. And where my heart is too heavy to rise, be gentle with me, and lift it Yourself. Amen.

fields.body_html:
Turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel? EZEKIEL 33:11

In 1658 Baxter published a small book that outsold almost everything else he wrote. A Call to the Unconverted was addressed not to ministers or to mature believers but to people sitting in church every week who had never, so far as he could tell, been converted at all. It went through edition after edition, was translated into several languages within his lifetime, and Baxter received reports of conversions from it for the rest of his life — including from places he had never visited.

The verse that governs it

The whole book is an exposition of one verse, and the choice tells us a great deal about his instincts.

Say unto them, As I live, saith the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live. EZEKIEL 33:11

Baxter fastened on three things in it. God swears. As I live is an oath, and Baxter asked what it means that God should take an oath about His own disposition towards sinners. It means the matter has been disputed, and that God is answering the charge. God denies taking pleasure in their ruin. Baxter thought this the most commonly disbelieved sentence in Scripture — not intellectually denied, but practically disbelieved by people who imagine that God is looking for a reason to condemn them and will not be sorry when He finds one. And God pleads. The doubling — turn ye, turn ye — is the language of someone who will not take silence for an answer.

Why will ye die?

The refrain of the book is the question at the end of the verse, and Baxter turned it over and over, because he regarded it as unanswerable. Nobody has a reason. The man who will not turn cannot produce an account of himself that would survive five minutes of honest examination. He is not choosing hell; he is postponing the subject, which comes to the same thing in the end. Baxter’s method throughout is to reason with the reader rather than to work on him. He anticipates objections and answers them. He asks what the reader is gaining by delay, what he expects to be different next year, whether he supposes he will have more inclination then or less, and what he intends to say when asked to account for the delay.

Behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation. 2 CORINTHIANS 6:2

Earnestness without manipulation

There is a distinction here worth noticing, because evangelistic urgency has a long history of going wrong. Baxter is enormously earnest. He pleads; he repeats himself; he presses the reader with the shortness of life and the certainty of judgment. And he does it entirely by argument and appeal to the conscience. There is no working of the emotions for their own sake, no engineered crisis, no technique for producing a response in a meeting. The difference matters. Manipulation produces decisions that dissolve within a month, and it leaves the manipulated person harder than before, because he has now been inoculated. Baxter aimed at the understanding and the conscience, trusting that if a man genuinely saw his situation he would act.

Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:11

Persuade is the word. It assumes a mind that can be reached.

Written for people who could not read it

One detail about the book’s circulation is worth recording, because it explains Baxter’s whole approach to publishing. He wrote deliberately in plain language for poor readers, kept the price low, and gave copies away in quantity. He urged wealthy Christians to buy stocks of such books and distribute them, and he did the same himself with a good deal of his own income. In a parish where many could not read at all, he expected the literate to read aloud to the household. The book is written to be heard as much as read — the sentences are direct, the arguments repeat, and the address is personal throughout.

How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? ROMANS 10:14

A note on his doctrine here

Readers acquainted with the debates of Baxter’s century will notice that this book leans on the universality of the gospel call, and that Baxter defends the sincerity of God’s offer to all who hear it with more warmth than some of his strictly Calvinist contemporaries thought proper. He held a modified position on the extent of the atonement, and it shaped his evangelism. We shall come to the controversy in chapter six. It is enough here to say that whatever one concludes about the theology, Baxter’s practice is the one the New Testament models: a universal, urgent, sincere call to every hearer, without qualification and without hedging.

There is an application of this chapter that most readers will want to avoid, and it is the obvious one. You know someone who is not converted. You see them regularly. You have never raised it, because the moment never seems right and you do not want to damage the relationship. Baxter’s question is not whether the moment is right. It is what you will say about the delay.

What delay actually is

Baxter devoted considerable space to the commonest response his book met, which was not rejection but postponement. Almost nobody, he observed, decides against Christ. What people do is agree in principle and defer in practice — intending to attend to the matter later, when life is less pressing, when the children are older, when the business is settled. He regarded this as the most dangerous condition a person can be in, precisely because it feels reasonable and produces no alarm.

And as he reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled, and answered, Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee. ACTS 24:25

Felix is the pattern. He was moved — he trembled — and he postponed, and so far as the record goes the convenient season never arrived. Baxter’s argument against delay ran on three lines. You have no lease on the time. The assumption that the matter can be attended to later depends on a future nobody has been promised. You will not be more inclined then. Every year of postponement makes the thing harder, not easier, because habits set and consciences grow quieter.

But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin. HEBREWS 3:13

And you are, in the meantime, losing everything the delay costs — the peace, the usefulness, the years that might have been spent well. His conclusion was blunt. A man who intends to turn eventually has already conceded the argument and is merely haggling over the date, which is a remarkably poor thing to be doing with a life.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Name one person you see regularly who, so far as you can tell, is not converted. Write the name down. 2. Ask yourself Baxter’s own question about your silence: what are you gaining by the delay, and what do you expect to be different next year? 3. If you have been putting off your own turning to God, stop postponing. Nobody has a reason that survives examination. 4. Aim at the conscience, not the emotions. Reason with people; do not work on them. 5. Buy a plain, sound Christian book and give it away. It was one of Baxter’s most effective methods and it costs almost nothing.

A PRAYER
Lord God, You have sworn by Your own life that You take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and I have not believed it about myself or about anyone else.
Forgive my silence. There are people I see every week whose souls I have never once mentioned to them, and I have called my cowardice discretion.
Give me the earnestness that pleads and the honesty that reasons, and keep me from every technique that works on people rather than serving them.
And if there is any part of me still postponing, let me settle it now. Amen.

fields.title: The Nature of True Conversion
fields.body_html:
Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven. MATTHEW 7:21

Having spent a book calling people to turn, Baxter spent another explaining what turning actually is — because he was convinced that a large proportion of the people in English parish churches believed themselves Christians on grounds that would not bear examination.

What conversion is not

He began by clearing away the false marks, and the list is uncomfortably current. It is not being born into a Christian family, baptised, and taught the catechism. It is not moral respectability, which many unconverted people possess in greater measure than many converted ones. It is not orthodoxy of opinion — a man may hold every article correctly and be unchanged. It is not religious feeling, however strong; Baxter had watched people weep under preaching and return to their old lives within the week. And it is not the performance of religious duty, which can be maintained for a lifetime out of habit, fear or social necessity.

Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? …And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you. MATTHEW 7:22–23

Baxter regarded that passage as the most sobering in the Bible for religious people, on the grounds that the persons addressed are not sceptics or scandalous sinners but active and apparently successful workers.

Three things that change

His positive account is unusually clear, and it is worth learning because it gives a believer something to examine himself by that is not a feeling. Conversion, in Baxter’s analysis, is a change in three related things. A change of ultimate end. Every person is living for something — an aim which organises the rest. For the unconverted man, whatever his religion, that aim is finally himself: his comfort, his standing, his security, his pleasure. In conversion the end changes, and God takes the place the self occupied.

A change of chief good. Related but distinct. Every person has something he treats as his real happiness — the thing whose loss would ruin him. Baxter’s test was to ask what a man would be unable to live without. Conversion is the transfer of that place to God.

Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. PSALM 73:25

A change of governing master. The convert has changed sides. He is no longer his own, and the will of Christ has become the authority to which disputes are referred.

To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God. ACTS 26:18

God’s work and ours

Baxter held both sides firmly, and he was attacked from both directions for it. Conversion is God’s work. Nobody turns himself; the change described above is not within the reach of a will that is itself part of the problem.

A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh. EZEKIEL 36:26

And conversion is genuinely the sinner’s act. He turns; he repents; he believes. These are not things done to a passive object, and Scripture commands them of everyone who hears. Baxter refused to resolve the tension by dropping either half, and he was impatient with those who did. To the man who said he could not turn, Baxter answered that nothing was preventing him but his own unwillingness. To the man who thought he could manage it whenever convenient, Baxter answered that he had never yet managed the smallest part of it and had better cry to God for help.

Gradual and definite

One further point, and it saves a good deal of unnecessary distress. Baxter did not require that a believer be able to name the date of his conversion. He knew that many are brought up in godly homes and cannot identify a moment, and that the work is often gradual and only recognisable afterwards. What he insisted on is that the change itself must be real and present, whatever its history. The question is not when did it happen? but has it happened? — and that question is answered by examining what a person now lives for, treats as his happiness, and obeys.

Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:17

A caution before the applications, because this chapter can wound the wrong people. Searching self-examination is medicine for the confident and poison for the fearful. Believers of tender conscience frequently fail every test they apply to themselves and conclude they are lost, while the genuinely unconverted sail through unbothered. If you are the sort of person who is already anxious about this, take the chapter gently, and read chapter fifteen before you go further.

The soil without depth

Baxter drew heavily on the parable of the sower, and particularly on the second soil, because it describes a person who looks converted and is not.

But he that received the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it; yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended. MATTHEW 13:20–21

Every detail matters. The response is immediate. It is joyful — more visibly enthusiastic, often, than that of the good soil. It is genuine as far as it goes; the man is not pretending. And it does not last. The diagnosis is given in four words: no root in himself. Something happened at the surface which never reached the depth, and the plant was living on borrowed moisture. Baxter’s practical application was to warn against judging by early enthusiasm, either in others or in oneself. The most reliable evidence is time, and time cannot be hurried. He also identified what typically exposes the difference: tribulation or persecution. Trouble is the test, because a religion adopted for what it supplies — comfort, belonging, a better life — has no reason to persist once it begins to cost. The pastoral counsel that follows is patience. New believers should be received warmly and watched quietly, not promoted quickly. And a person who has fallen away is not to be written off; the parable describes what happened, not what must always happen. Roots can still go down.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask what you are actually living for — not what you would say, but what your decisions reveal. 2. Identify what you could not live without. That is your chief good, whatever your theology says. 3. Notice where you refer disputes. When your will and Christ’s conflict, which one wins in practice? 4. Do not fret over the date. Ask whether the change is present, not when it began. 5. If this examination is crushing rather than clarifying, stop, and take it to a wise believer rather than continuing alone.

A PRAYER
Lord, I have called myself a Christian on grounds I have never examined, and I would rather know the truth now than discover it too late.
Show me what I am living for. Show me what I treat as my real happiness. Show me who wins when Your will and mine collide.
If I have never truly turned, turn me. I cannot do it, and I will not pretend I can; but I am asking, which is the one thing I can do.
And if I am Yours, quiet the fear that keeps accusing me, and let me rest in what You have done. Amen.

fields.body_html:
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law. ROMANS 3:28

This is the chapter in which Baxter must be read most carefully, because it deals with the point on which most of his own party judged him to have gone wrong. It would be easy to leave it out. It is left out of most popular treatments of him. But a book that presented Baxter’s pastoral genius while quietly omitting the doctrine that made him a byword for controversy would not be honest, and the reader would meet it eventually anyway.

What he was reacting against

Baxter’s position was formed in the army, and that matters. As a chaplain in the New Model Army in the mid-1640s he encountered opinions that horrified him — among them a species of Antinomianism which held that since the believer is justified by the imputed righteousness of Christ, his own conduct is in no way a condition of anything. Baxter saw men drawing the practical conclusion, and he never forgot it. His Aphorisms of Justification, published in 1649, was written to close that door. It opened a controversy that occupied him, on and off, for the rest of his life.

What he taught

Set out as fairly as possible, his position ran roughly as follows. Christ’s death satisfied God’s justice and procured a new covenant — a covenant of grace, whose terms are faith and repentance rather than perfect obedience. The sinner is justified not by keeping the old law, which he cannot, but by meeting the conditions of the new one, which by grace he can. On this account, faith justifies as the appointed condition of the covenant rather than merely as the instrument that receives Christ’s righteousness. And Baxter spoke of a personal, evangelical righteousness — consisting in sincere faith and repentance — alongside the righteousness of Christ, which he did not deny but understood differently from his critics. He also held a modified view of the atonement, that Christ died sufficiently for all and effectually for those who believe.

His motive throughout was pastoral. He was trying to secure the necessity of holiness against men who had made grace an excuse.

Why it was resisted

The objections came quickly, from John Owen among others, and they have been repeated ever since. They deserve to be stated plainly. If faith justifies as a condition we perform, then it is difficult to see how it has not become a work — the very thing Paul excludes in the passages where the doctrine is defined.

But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness. ROMANS 4:5

If our sincere faith and repentance constitute a personal righteousness that contributes to our standing, then the ground of acceptance has shifted, at least partly, from Christ to us — and the believer’s assurance now depends on the adequacy of his own sincerity, which is precisely what the doctrine was meant to remove.

And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith. PHILIPPIANS 3:9

And the practical effect, critics argued, is the opposite of what Baxter intended. A believer who is uncertain whether his repentance has been sincere enough cannot rest, and a religion of anxious self-inspection is not more holy than one of settled faith. It is merely more miserable. Baxter’s later followers pressed his views further than he did, and the resulting controversy over what came to be called neonomianism divided English Nonconformity for generations.

Where this book stands

It would be evasive to set out both sides and decline to say anything. The judgment of the great majority of Reformed theologians, then and since, is that Baxter erred here — that his concern to protect holiness was right, that his remedy compromised the freeness of justification, and that the New Testament secures holiness by a different route, namely union with Christ, which produces obedience as fruit rather than requiring it as a condition.

For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works. EPHESIANS 2:8–10

Paul secures both in three verses, and the order is decisive. Works follow; they do not condition.

What is not in dispute

Having said that, three things should be added, and they matter. Baxter was not preaching salvation by works, and it is a caricature to say so. He insisted on grace, on Christ’s satisfaction, and on the impossibility of earning anything. The dispute was about the precise role of faith within a system all parties agreed was gracious. His pastoral concern was legitimate and remains so. Antinomianism is a real disease, not a bogey; every generation produces Christians who treat forgiveness as permission. And on everything else in this book — the ministry, heaven, catechising, family religion, the use of time — Baxter is a safe and superb guide. A man may be wrong at one point and reliable at fifty others, which is true of every teacher any of us has ever had.

The practical counsel is simple. On this question, follow Paul rather than Baxter. Rest your acceptance wholly on Christ’s righteousness, received by faith which is itself God’s gift, and let holiness grow from that security rather than be required as its price.

What both sides agreed

Before leaving this controversy it is worth stating what was not in dispute, because heated debates make participants sound further apart than they are. Every party held that salvation is by grace. Nobody in the argument thought a sinner could earn acceptance with God, and nobody was proposing a religion of merit. Baxter would have rejected such a suggestion as forcefully as his critics. Every party held that Christ’s death is the sole ground of forgiveness. The dispute concerned how its benefits are conveyed and what part faith plays, not whether the cross was sufficient.

For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; who gave himself a ransom for all. 1 TIMOTHY 2:5–6

Every party held that faith is itself the gift of God, not a contribution the sinner produces from his own resources. And every party held that genuine faith produces holiness. Baxter’s critics were not Antinomians; they simply located the necessity of obedience elsewhere in the system than he did — as the fruit of union with Christ rather than as a condition of the covenant.

Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord. HEBREWS 12:14

The disagreement was real and it mattered, and this book has said where it thinks the weight of the argument lies. But it was a disagreement between men who agreed on a great deal, conducted with a sharpness that obscured the agreement — which is, as it happens, exactly what Baxter complained about when other people did it.

Notice which error you personally drift towards — treating grace as permission, or treating faith as a performance — and correct in the other direction. 3. Read Ephesians 2:8–10 and mark the order. Works follow; they do not condition. 4. Practise holding a teacher’s error and his usefulness together. It is a skill every reader needs. 5. When assurance wobbles, look outward to Christ rather than inward to your sincerity.

A PRAYER
Father, I want to be holy, and I keep trying to secure it by making my acceptance depend on my performance — and then I have neither holiness nor peace.
Let my standing rest wholly on Christ. Not on the sincerity of my repentance, not on the strength of my faith, but on Him.
And out of that security, make me obedient. Let good works grow from what You have done rather than be demanded as the price of it.
Guard me from treating Your grace as permission. Guard me equally from treating Your gospel as a new law. Amen.

fields.title: Take Heed to Yourselves
fields.body_html:
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers. ACTS 20:28

In 1656 Baxter published a book intended for the ministers of Worcestershire, written to accompany their agreement to take up systematic personal instruction in their parishes. It was an occasional piece for a local purpose. It has never been out of print since, and it is still set for theological students three and a half centuries later. The Reformed Pastor takes its structure from Paul’s charge at Miletus, and it follows the order of the text exactly. Take heed to yourselves comes first. Baxter would not let anyone reverse it.

The unconverted minister

He opened with a possibility that most books on ministry decline to raise: that a man may hold office, preach competently, be respected by his people, and be unconverted. Baxter thought this was neither rare nor hypothetical. A man may enter the ministry as a career, learn its vocabulary fluently, and never once have dealt with God on his own account. He may spend his life urging others to a place he has not been.

Thou therefore which teachest another, teachest thou not thyself? ROMANS 2:21
But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway. 1 CORINTHIANS 9:27

That verse is Paul’s, about Paul. Baxter’s point was that if the apostle considered the danger worth naming, no minister since has grounds for complacency.

Preaching against sins you live in

His second warning is subtler and touches everyone who teaches. It is entirely possible, Baxter observed, to preach against a sin with real force while practising it. The pulpit provides a curious immunity: a man denouncing covetousness is not, at that moment, thinking of himself, and the very act of condemning the fault can produce a comfortable sense of being on the right side of it.

He was specific about the ministerial versions. Pride he named as the chief — pride in gifts, in learning, in reputation, in the size of a congregation, in being thought humble. Laziness, disguised as study. Worldliness, disguised as prudence about money. And contentiousness, disguised as zeal for truth. That last one he applied to himself without hesitation, and anyone who has read his controversial writings will agree that the diagnosis was accurate.

And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye? MATTHEW 7:3

The example

Baxter’s third emphasis is that a minister teaches chiefly by what he is. The congregation is watching, and it learns more from how a man treats his family, handles money, responds to criticism and speaks of his opponents than from anything he says in a sermon. A discrepancy between the two is noticed immediately, and it does more damage than any amount of poor preaching.

Be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity. 1 TIMOTHY 4:12

He drew the practical conclusion that a minister’s private devotion is not a personal matter. A man who neglects his own soul is not merely damaging himself; he is depriving his people, because he can only give what he has.

Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee. 1 TIMOTHY 4:16

A necessary caution

Now a warning about the book itself, because it must be said. The Reformed Pastor is one of the most searching books in the English language and one of the most crushing. Baxter’s standard is extraordinarily high, his tone is relentless, and he shows very little interest in comforting the reader. Ministers who are already conscientious — which is to say, exactly the ministers who read it — have been driven by it into despair and, in some cases, out of the ministry altogether. That was not his intention, and it is a misuse of the book. Baxter was writing to rouse men who had grown complacent, not to finish off men who were already at the end of themselves. The safeguard is to read it with the gospel in the other hand. Every failure it exposes is a failure Christ has already borne. A minister who reads it and is convicted should repent and change one thing; a minister who reads it and despairs has forgotten that his acceptance was never based on his performance in the first place.

There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus. ROMANS 8:1

Not only for ministers

One further note, because most readers of this book are not pastors. Everything in this chapter applies, at a smaller scale, to anyone who teaches anyone — a parent, a Sunday school teacher, an elder, a small group leader, an older believer who has taken a younger one under their wing. The order is the same. Take heed to yourself first. What you are will reach the people in your care more surely than what you say, and the discrepancy between the two, if there is one, will be noticed long before you notice it.

Baxter’s most useful question for anyone who teaches is short and can be asked tonight. Is there anything you regularly urge on others that you are not currently practising yourself?

Two particular pressures

Baxter singled out two areas where ministers most often fail, and both are places where the failure is visible to everyone except the man himself. The first is his household. Paul makes the connection explicit and gives the reason.

One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity; (for if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?) 1 TIMOTHY 3:4–5

Baxter observed that a man may give his best hours to the parish and arrive home with nothing left, so that the people who most need him receive the worst of him. He regarded this as a straightforward failure of duty rather than a regrettable side effect of zeal, and he warned that a congregation is not deceived by it for long. The second is money. Not, usually, dramatic dishonesty — but the slow accommodation by which a man’s standard of living, ambitions and choice of associates come to be shaped by financial interest without his ever having made a decision about it.

Not greedy of filthy lucre, but of a ready mind; neither as being lords over God’s heritage, but being ensamples to the flock. 1 PETER 5:2–3

Baxter’s own practice was severe: he lived plainly, gave away a large part of a modest income, and refused preferment when it was offered. He did not require others to match him, and he did require that the question be faced. His test was to ask whether any decision in a man’s ministry over the last year had been influenced by what it would cost him. The answer, honestly given, is usually informative.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Name one thing you regularly urge on others and are not doing. Begin doing it this week. 2. Examine yourself for the four ministerial sins — pride, laziness, worldliness, contentiousness — and identify which is yours. 3. Ask whether your own devotional life exists independently of your preparation to teach. If not, that is the finding. 4. If this chapter crushes you rather than convicting you, stop and read Romans 8:1. Change one thing; do not despair. 5. If you have never settled the question of your own conversion, settle it before you teach anyone else anything.

A PRAYER
Lord, I have urged on others what I do not practise, and I have denounced sins from a position that felt safe while I was denouncing them.
Search me. Show me the pride I have dressed up as conviction, the laziness I have called study, the love of money I have called prudence, the quarrelsomeness I have called zeal.
Keep my own soul, so that I have something to give. Let me take heed to myself before I take heed to anyone else.
And when I see how far short I fall, do not let me despair. My standing was never built on my performance. Amen.

fields.title: Take Heed to All the Flock
fields.body_html:
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly. 1 PETER 5:2

The second half of Paul’s charge governs the second half of Baxter’s book, and he fastened on one word in it: all.

Every single one

Take heed to all the flock. Not the responsive ones, not the ones who attend regularly, not the ones whose conversation is agreeable or whose support is useful. All of them. Baxter took this to mean that a minister is responsible for every individual in his charge by name, and that he cannot discharge that responsibility from a pulpit alone. Preaching addresses a congregation; oversight requires knowing people. He was blunt about the arithmetic. If a parish is too large for its minister to know its members individually, then either he must obtain help or the parish must be divided — but he may not simply preach at a crowd and call it oversight, because that is not what the word means.

And I will set up shepherds over them which shall feed them: and they shall fear no more, nor be dismayed, neither shall they be lacking. JEREMIAH 23:4

The weight of it

Baxter’s motivation was an accountability he could not get out of his mind.

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account. HEBREWS 13:17

Baxter set out what he thought the work actually required, and it is a heavy list. fields.title: The Work of Catechising
fields.body_html:
And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house. ACTS 20:20

Here is the practice that made Kidderminster famous, and it is the most transferable thing Baxter ever did. He and his assistant set aside two full days every week for personal instruction. Families came to his house by appointment, one household at a time. He went through the essentials of the Christian faith with them, asked what they understood, corrected what they had wrong, and dealt with each person about the state of their own soul. They worked through around fourteen families a week and covered the whole parish — some eight hundred families — in a year. Then they began again.

Why preaching was not enough

Baxter loved preaching and was good at it. His argument was not against it but about its limits. From a pulpit you cannot tell what has been understood. People sit through sermons for decades, nodding, and turn out on examination to hold a confused folk-religion assembled from fragments. Baxter reported the experience of discovering that respectable parishioners of long standing could not say who Christ was or what He had done, having heard him preach both weekly for years. Personal instruction solves this because it is two-way. The person has to answer. Their actual understanding becomes visible, and you can address what is genuinely there rather than what you assumed.

Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus. COLOSSIANS 1:28

Baxter noticed that Paul says every man three times in one verse, and concluded that the apostolic method was individual as well as public.

What he found

His reported results were startling and he was careful about them. He said that he learned more about his people in one hour of personal conversation than in years of preaching to them, and that more apparent conversions followed this work than followed his public ministry — though he added, honestly, that the preaching had prepared much of what the conversation harvested. He also found the work humbling. Ministers who take it up generally discover that their preaching has been aimed at a congregation that does not exist: better informed, more attentive and less confused than the actual people in the pews.

The practicalities

Baxter was characteristically detailed about the method, and the details are what make it usable. Give them something first. He supplied each family with a printed catechism ahead of the visit, so they knew what would be discussed and could prepare. He bought these and distributed them himself. Take them one household at a time. Privacy matters. People will not admit ignorance in front of neighbours, and will not discuss their souls in a crowd. Begin with knowledge, and move to the conscience. Establish what they understand, then apply it personally — what does this mean for you, and where are you in relation to it? Be gentle with the ignorant. Baxter insisted on this. Shaming a person for not knowing something guarantees they will never tell you the truth again. Keep records, so that the next round can build on the last.

And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way. DEUTERONOMY 6:7

The objections he answered

He anticipated the excuses, and they are still the ones we use. There is no time. Baxter’s reply was that there is time for whatever we consider essential, and that a man who cannot find two days a week for the souls in his charge should examine what the other days are going to. The people will not come. At Kidderminster nearly all of them did, once it was explained and expected. He acknowledged that in other places they might not, and answered that a minister is responsible for offering, not for the response. It is not my gift. Baxter regarded this as the least respectable of the objections. The work does not require unusual gifts. It requires knowing the faith, caring about people, and being willing to spend the hours.

Most readers of this book are not clergy, and the practice adapts. Any believer can do this with one other person: a child, a new convert, a friend who is curious, someone in the congregation younger than themselves. Take a short catechism or a book of the Bible, meet regularly, ask what they understand rather than telling them what they should, and press it home gently. It is the least glamorous method in Christian history, and it has a better record than most of the others.

What to teach

Baxter was specific about the content of personal instruction, and his structure is worth having because it prevents the whole exercise from wandering. He worked from the traditional four heads, which Protestants and Catholics alike had used for generations and which cover the ground with remarkable economy. The Creed — what a Christian believes. Who God is, what He has done in creation and redemption, who Christ is, what the Spirit does, what the church is, and what is coming. The Ten Commandments — how a Christian lives. Baxter used these not as a ladder to be climbed but as a mirror, to show a person his need, and then as a map, to show him the shape of obedience. The Lord’s Prayer — what a Christian asks for. He found this the most useful of the four for exposing the state of a heart, since what a person wants reveals more than what he professes. And the sacraments — baptism and the Lord’s Supper, what they mean and what is required of those who come.

Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus. 2 TIMOTHY 1:13

The great advantage of a fixed structure is that it prevents a teacher from following his own enthusiasms. Left to ourselves we teach what interests us, and whole areas go untouched for years. A settled framework guarantees that everyone receives the whole of it. Baxter added one instruction that governs the rest: do not merely establish that a person can repeat the words. Ask what each clause means, and what difference it makes to them. A parishioner who could recite the Creed perfectly and had no idea what any of it signified was, in his experience, the commonest discovery of all.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Choose one person and begin meeting with them regularly to go through the Christian faith. Start this month. 2. Ask questions rather than delivering content. You cannot address what you have not discovered. 3. Give them something to prepare from — a catechism, a book, a passage — so the meeting has a spine. 4. Be gentle with ignorance. Shame ends honesty permanently. 5. If you lead a church, audit how much of your ministry is one-directional. Then change one thing about your diary.

A PRAYER
Lord, I have spoken a great deal and discovered very little about what the people around me actually believe.
Give me the patience for the slow work — one person at a time, asking rather than telling, learning what is really there before I try to correct it.
Make me gentle with those who know little. Let no one be ashamed to admit their ignorance to me.
And give me the diligence to keep at it when it is unremarkable and nobody is watching. Amen.
