fields.title: Family Religion
fields.body_html:
But as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. JOSHUA 24:15

Baxter held a conviction that runs through his entire practical theology and that he stated as bluntly as he could: that the reformation of the church depends on the reformation of families, and that a nation of godly households would need very little else. He was not being rhetorical. In A Christian Directory he devoted an entire part to the ordering of households, and he wrote a separate volume for poor families who could afford nothing longer.

The household as the first church

His argument was that God has arranged the world so that most religious formation happens at home, whatever the church does. A person spends an hour or two a week under preaching and the rest of his life in a household. If the two contradict each other, the household wins. Children raised in a home where religion is professed on Sunday and absent from Monday to Saturday learn, accurately, that it is a social observance.

For I know him, that he will command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the Lord. GENESIS 18:19

Baxter noticed that God’s commendation of Abraham is not about his faith in the abstract but about what he would do with his household. Similarly, the qualification for an elder turns on the same point.

One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity; (for if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?) 1 TIMOTHY 3:4–5

The head of the house as its minister

From this Baxter drew a conclusion that many Christians still find surprising: the head of a household has a genuinely pastoral office within it. He is to teach the faith to those in his care, pray with them, examine what they understand, correct them, and set the example. Baxter regarded this not as an optional enthusiasm for the unusually devout but as a plain duty attached to the position.

And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. EPHESIANS 6:4

Note both halves. The instruction is commanded; so is the manner of it. Baxter was firm that harsh, hectoring family religion produces the opposite of what it intends, and he warned parents that a child driven to resent the faith may carry that resentment for life.

What it actually looked like

He was practical about the shape of it, and the shape is simple enough to adopt this week. A fixed time, kept daily, so that it does not depend on anyone remembering or feeling like it. Baxter favoured morning and evening; one is better than none. Everyone present — children, servants, lodgers. The household means the household. Reading, a short passage, read aloud. Instruction, brief and pitched at the youngest person in the room rather than the oldest. Baxter was emphatic on this. A father who conducts family worship at the level of his own understanding is talking to himself. Prayer, short, specific and audible — covering the day’s actual business rather than generalities. Singing, where the household can manage it. Above all, brief. Baxter warned that long family devotions produce children who dread the hour, and that a short exercise faithfully kept accomplishes far more than a long one abandoned within a fortnight.

That the generation to come might know them, even the children which should be born; who should arise and declare them to their children. PSALM 78:6

Where the household is divided

A qualification Baxter’s own century needed less than ours does. Many readers are not in a position to institute family worship. A believing wife with an unbelieving husband, a young person in a hostile home, a single person, a worker in someone else’s household — the pattern above assumes an authority they do not have. The New Testament addresses exactly this situation, and its counsel is not to force the issue.

Likewise, ye wives, be in subjection to your own husbands; that, if any obey not the word, they also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives. 1 PETER 3:1

Without the word — won by conduct rather than argument. A believer in a divided household may pray privately, live consistently, take whatever opportunity is given, and leave the rest to God without concluding that they have failed.

The long view

One further encouragement, since family religion is the least immediately rewarding thing most Christians do. It is almost entirely invisible. Nobody applauds it. Its results, if they come, appear twenty years later in the character of people who will not remember where they got it. A parent conducting a short reading and prayer with distracted children on a wet Tuesday evening has no evidence that anything is happening, and usually feels faintly ridiculous. Baxter’s answer was that God has appointed means, and that we are responsible for the means rather than the outcome.

And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. GALATIANS 6:9

If your household has no regular time of worship, the useful thing to take from this chapter is not a conviction but an appointment. Choose the time before you put the book down.

The whole household

A word about the word household, because it meant something broader in Baxter’s century than it does in ours, and the breadth is worth recovering. The households he addressed included servants, apprentices, journeymen and lodgers — people who lived under the roof and worked in the business without being related to anyone. Baxter’s instructions to heads of households cover all of them without distinction. The apprentice was to be taught and prayed for exactly as the son was.

A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway. ACTS 10:2

Cornelius is commended for the state of his whole house, and when Peter arrives he finds a room full of relatives and close friends assembled to hear. The modern application is not obvious but it is real. Few readers employ live-in apprentices. Most have some equivalent — a lodger, a student, an elderly relative, a neighbour’s child who is always in the kitchen, a colleague who comes for meals, an employee whose life you know something about.

Baxter’s principle was that responsibility follows proximity. The people whose lives regularly intersect with yours are, to some degree, your charge, whether or not the arrangement is formal. The practical form of this is hospitality, and Scripture commands it more often than we generally notice.

Use hospitality one to another without grudging. 1 PETER 4:9

A household where the faith is quietly practised, and to which people are regularly invited, does an evangelistic work that no programme can duplicate — because what visitors observe over a dinner table cannot be staged.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Fix a daily time for household worship and start tomorrow. Ten minutes is enough. 2. Pitch it at the youngest person present, not the oldest. 3. Keep it short. A brief exercise sustained for years beats a long one abandoned in a month. 4. Check your manner. Are you provoking the people you are trying to instruct? 5. fields.title: The Life of Faith
fields.body_html:
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. HEBREWS 11:1

Baxter preached a sermon before the king in 1660 on the life of faith, and afterwards expanded it into one of his most useful books. Its thesis is a diagnosis of the ordinary Christian’s real problem, and it is not the one we usually name.

The problem is not doubt

We assume that a believer’s difficulty is intellectual — that he is troubled by objections and needs his questions answered. Baxter thought this was true of very few. The great majority of Christians, he argued, do not doubt the doctrines at all. They affirm them sincerely, would defend them if challenged, and are entirely unaffected by them. The problem is not disbelief but unreality. We hold that God is present, that heaven is coming, that souls are eternal — and we live as though the visible world were the only solid one, because it is the one that presses on our senses every waking moment.

While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:18

Baxter’s illustration was the difference between a man who knows there is a fire in the next street and a man who can see it. Both believe the same fact. Only one is moving.

Faith as a second sight

His definition of faith follows from this. Faith is the faculty by which the unseen world becomes as real to us as the seen one — not more certain, since God’s word is more certain than our eyes, but as present. The chapter he worked from is Hebrews 11, and he pointed out what is said of Moses.

By faith he forsook Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king: for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible. HEBREWS 11:27

As seeing him who is invisible. That is the whole matter in a phrase. Moses acted against every visible consideration because something invisible was more real to him. And of the patriarchs:

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them. HEBREWS 11:13

Baxter drew out the sequence: they saw, they were persuaded, they embraced. Sight first — the sight faith gives — and conduct followed from it.

Where it bites

The practical value of this analysis is that it redirects our efforts. If our problem were doubt, the remedy would be argument. Since our problem is unreality, the remedy is attention — and this is exactly why Baxter placed such weight on meditation. The unseen becomes real to the person who deliberately attends to it, and stays theoretical for everyone else. He applied it in several directions. To money. A man who genuinely saw the two worlds would find the calculations easy. The difficulty is not that we think the heavenly treasure inferior; it is that we cannot see it, and the visible pound is here in the hand. To suffering. Paul’s arithmetic in 2 Corinthians 4 — a light affliction, working an eternal weight of glory — is not consolation offered against the evidence. It is a sober comparison, available to anyone who can see both terms. To death. Baxter, who expected his own for fifty years, held that the fear of dying is largely a failure of sight. What is feared is a vacancy, because the other side is not being looked at.

Living by faith daily

He was practical about how faith is exercised, and it comes down to a habit of recall. The believer, several times a day, deliberately calls to mind what is actually the case: that God is present in this room; that the person in front of him will exist for ever; that this hour is being recorded; that Christ is at the right hand of God and is not indifferent to what is happening here. None of that is new information. It is the deliberate application of information already held, and Baxter thought the whole difference between a vigorous Christian and a dull one lies in whether it is done.

I have set the Lord always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved. PSALM 16:8

There is a test in this that anyone can apply honestly. Consider something you say you believe — that God sees you, or that you will give account, or that heaven is real. Then look at your last week and ask what you would have done differently if you had not believed it. If the answer is nothing, the belief is not yet operative, and the remedy is not more information.

Faith and the promises

If faith is living by the unseen, the question is what it holds on to — and Baxter’s answer was: particular promises, in particular words. He was impatient with a faith that consisted of general good feeling about God’s character. Feelings about God fluctuate; a sentence He has spoken does not.

Whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature. 2 PETER 1:4

His counsel was to gather promises deliberately — to know where they are, to write them down, to have particular ones for particular troubles, so that when the trouble arrives the search does not have to begin then. Abraham is the model, and Paul is careful about the mechanism.

He staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God; and being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform. ROMANS 4:20–21

Two things anchor him: a promise that was made, and a God who is able. Nothing in the account depends on Abraham’s feelings, which by the evidence of Genesis were frequently poor. Baxter added a distinction that saves a good deal of confusion. Some promises are absolute and belong to every believer without condition — forgiveness, the Spirit’s indwelling, final preservation. Others are attached to conditions, and some concern outcomes God has not committed Himself to in any particular case. Claiming the second sort as though they were the first produces disappointment and, eventually, the conclusion that God does not keep His word. Know which is which. Then hold the first without any hesitation at all.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Take one doctrine you affirm and ask what you would have done differently last week had you not believed it. Sit with the answer. 2. Practise deliberate recall three times tomorrow: God is present here; this person is eternal; this hour is being recorded. 3. Where a decision about money is difficult, name both terms of the comparison honestly. The difficulty is usually one of sight, not of principle. 4. When afraid, ask whether you are looking at the trouble and not at God. Then look. 5. Stop treating your problem as intellectual if it is not. Give the time you would have spent on arguments to attention instead.

A PRAYER
Lord, I believe a great many things that have made no difference to me, and I have called that faith.
My trouble is not that I doubt You. It is that You are not real to me in the way this room is real, and so I live by what I can see.
Give me the sight that faith gives. Let me endure as seeing Him who is invisible.
Bring the unseen close today — Your presence, the worth of the people around me, the account I shall give — and let it change what I actually do. Amen.

fields.title: Self-Examination
fields.body_html:
Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. 2 CORINTHIANS 13:5

Baxter was a physician of souls in an almost literal sense — he studied medicine, catalogued his own ailments with clinical precision, and applied the same method to the inner life. Diagnosis before treatment. He held that most Christians never examine themselves at all, that a minority examine themselves destructively, and that a small number do it well. The distinction between the last two is the burden of this chapter.

Why it is commanded

Scripture requires it, and Baxter began there.

Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the Lord. LAMENTATIONS 3:40
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup. 1 CORINTHIANS 11:28

The reason it is necessary is the one Scripture also gives: we cannot be trusted to know ourselves without effort.

The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? JEREMIAH 17:9

Baxter took the second clause seriously. The heart is not merely corrupt; it is corrupt in a way that conceals itself from its owner. Which means that a comfortable general impression of oneself is worth very little, and that the matter requires deliberate work.

The method

He recommended a set practice, and it is unglamorous. A fixed time, preferably daily, at the end of the day, before sleep. He thought weekly review too infrequent, since by then most of the material has been forgotten. Specific questions, rather than a general trawl. Baxter supplied lists; the value is in their concreteness. How did I use this day? Where did I sin, and in what did it begin? What did I neglect that I ought to have done? What was I angry about, and what does that reveal? How did I treat the people in my house? Where was I proud? Did I speak of anyone in a way I would not repeat to their face?

Commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still. PSALM 4:4

Confession as you go, rather than accumulating a list. The point of the exercise is not to compile evidence but to deal with what is found. And a resolution, small and specific, for tomorrow.

The invitation that makes it safe

Here is the element that distinguishes healthy self-examination from morbid introspection, and Baxter knew it well.

Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: and see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting. PSALM 139:23–24

Notice that David does not examine himself alone. He asks God to do it. This changes everything about the exercise. A person searching his own heart by himself is using a faculty that is part of the problem, and he will either find too little or too much depending on his temperament. A person inviting God to search him is in company, and the searching is conducted by Someone who already knows the worst and has not withdrawn. Note also where the psalm ends: lead me in the way everlasting. The purpose is forward movement, not an inventory.

When it goes wrong

Baxter was unusually alert to the failure mode, and this is one of the places where his pastoral wisdom is at its best. Self-examination is medicine for the presumptuous and poison for the fearful. The people who most need it are those who never do it; the people who do it most are frequently those who should do it less. A ten-der conscience, turned relentlessly inward, produces not holiness but paralysis — and it can slide into the condition Baxter called melancholy, which is the subject of chapter fifteen. His safeguards are worth stating. Examine yourself at set times, and then stop. Do not carry the inquest through the day. Examine your conduct rather than your feelings. Feelings vary with health, weather and sleep, and prove very little. End by looking outward. The exercise should finish at Christ, not at yourself, because that is where the remedy is.

Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith. HEBREWS 12:2

And if you cannot do it without despair, do not do it alone. Take it to a wise believer who knows you.

The most practical thing here is the smallest. Tonight, before sleep, ask four questions about today, deal with what surfaces, and stop. Ten minutes, honestly spent, will show you more than a year of vague unease.

Watching the heart

One further emphasis, because Baxter thought it the point at which most self-examination is aimed too late.

Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life. PROVERBS 4:23

The proverb locates the work upstream. By the time a sin has reached speech or action it has already been forming for some while, and examining only the outcome is like inspecting a river at its mouth and wondering where the silt came from. Baxter’s counsel was to attend to beginnings. Not the angry word, but the resentment that had been maturing for a fortnight. Not the dishonest act, but the small compromise months earlier that made it thinkable. Not the affair, but the first conversation that was enjoyed more than it should have been. He observed that we generally know. Something registers at the time — a slight unease, a reluctance to mention it to anyone — and is overruled. That overruling, repeated, is how a conscience is trained into silence.

Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines. SONG OF SOLOMON 2:15

The practical form is to ask, in the nightly review, not only what was done but where it began. What was I thinking about while I waited? What did I turn over with pleasure? What did I decide not to mention? Baxter added an encouragement that keeps this from becoming oppressive. Watching the heart is not the same as distrusting every impulse. A believer whose heart has been renewed will find many of its motions good, and God is at work there. The discipline is one of attention rather than suspicion — noticing what is rising, in order to feed what is of God and starve what is not.

Coming to the Table

The New Testament attaches self-examination to one occasion in particular, and Baxter gave it corresponding weight.

But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup. 1 CORINTHIANS 11:28

The context is a congregation whose behaviour at the Lord’s Supper had become a scandal — divisions, the rich eating while the poor went without — and Paul’s instruction is that each person should look at himself before he comes. Baxter’s parishes observed a period of preparation before communion, which is where much of his personal instruction took place. The practice has largely lapsed, and something has been lost with it. But the examination Paul commands must be read carefully, because it is frequently turned into the opposite of its purpose. He does not tell the Corinthians to stay away until they are worthy; nobody would ever come. He tells them to examine themselves and so to eat. The examination is the road to the Table, not a barrier before it.

This is a faithful saying …that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief. 1 TIMOTHY 1:15

The questions to ask are therefore specific and limited. Am I trusting Christ? Is there any sin I am holding on to and intending to keep? Is there anyone here I am unreconciled with? That third question is the one Paul’s context presses hardest and the one we most often skip. A congregation that examined itself about its relationships before communion, rather than only about its private sins, would look rather different within a year.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Set a nightly time — ten minutes — and use specific questions rather than a general survey. 2. Ask God to do the searching rather than doing it alone. It is both safer and more accurate. 3. Confess as you go and finish with one small resolution for tomorrow. 4. Examine conduct rather than feelings. Feelings track your sleep more closely than your soul. 5. End by looking at Christ. If the exercise leaves you looking at yourself, you have stopped one step early.

A PRAYER
Lord, I know myself less well than I suppose, and my heart hides its worst from me.
I will not attempt this alone. Search me, O God, and know my heart. Show me what I did today, what I neglected, what I said, and what it came from.
Give me the honesty to see it and the faith to bring it straight to You rather than turning it over in the dark.
And lead me in the way everlasting — forward, not merely inward. Amen.

Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith. HEBREWS 12:2 And if you cannot do it without despair, do not do it alone. Take it to a wise believer who knows you. But the examination Paul commands must be read carefully, because it is frequently turned into the opposite of its purpose. He does not tell the Corinthians to stay away until they are worthy; nobody would ever come. He tells them to examine themselves and so to eat. The examination is the road to the Table, not a barrier before it. This is a faithful saying …that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief. 1 TIMOTHY 1:15 The questions to ask are therefore specific and limited. Am I trusting Christ? Is there any sin I am holding on to and intending to keep? Is there anyone here I am unreconciled with? That third question is the one Paul’s context presses hardest and the one we most often skip. I will not attempt this alone. Search me, O God, and know my heart. Show me what I did today, what I neglected, what I said, and what it came from. fields.body_html:
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world. GALATIANS 6:14

In 1658 Baxter published a treatise with a title that states its whole argument: The Crucifying of the World by the Cross of Christ. It is his fullest treatment of worldliness, and he regarded worldliness as the commonest and most respectable way of losing one’s soul.

A sin that is never named

His starting observation is that this is the one great sin about which the church is habitually silent. Congregations denounce drunkenness, dishonesty and immorality. Almost nobody preaches against the love of money, and almost nobody confesses it. Baxter thought this was not because the sin is rare but because it is universal among the respectable, and because it wears the clothes of prudence, providing for one’s family, and good stewardship.

Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. 1 JOHN 2:15

He was careful to define the term, because it is easy to caricature. Worldliness is not the possession of things, nor the enjoyment of them, nor the ordinary diligence by which a person feeds a household. God gives good things to be enjoyed with thanksgiving. Worldliness is the setting of the heart on them. It is treating this life’s goods as our portion rather than our provision — and Baxter’s test was to ask not what a man owns but what he could not bear to lose.

For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. MATTHEW 6:21

Why persuasion fails

Here is the argument that makes his treatment distinctive, and it is the reason for the title. Everyone already agrees that the world is passing. Preach a sermon on the vanity of riches and the congregation will nod; not one of them disputes it. And nothing changes, because the heart is not moved by information it already possesses.

The world’s grip, Baxter argued, is not broken by being told it is worthless. It is broken by a rival attachment, and the only thing strong enough is the cross.

By whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world. GALATIANS 6:14

Paul’s phrase runs both ways, and Baxter dwelt on the symmetry. The world is crucified to me: seen from the foot of the cross, its offers lose their appeal. I am crucified to the world: it no longer has anything to hold, because the person it used to bargain with has died. The practical method that follows is not resolution but contemplation. A man who wants to be free of the love of money will get further by an hour at Calvary than by an hour of resolving to be less greedy.

Prosperity is the harder test

Baxter made an observation that is uncomfortable in wealthy societies. Scripture treats poverty as a danger and prosperity as a greater one. The reason is that adversity drives people to God while comfort quietly persuades them they do not need Him — and does it so gradually that nobody notices the transition.

But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. 1 TIMOTHY 6:9

He noted that Paul does not say the rich but they that will be rich — those who have set their intention that way. The condition is one of ambition rather than balance. Baxter’s own practice matched his preaching. He lived simply, gave away a large part of a modest income, refused a bishopric, and bought books to distribute at his own expense in quantities he could not really afford.

What to do with what you have

He was not an ascetic, and his counsel is constructive rather than merely prohibitive.

Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy; that they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate. 1 TIMOTHY 6:17–18

Note that Paul commands enjoyment in the same breath as generosity. God gives things richly to enjoy, and a sour refusal of good gifts is not holiness.

Baxter’s directions were practical. Hold possessions as a steward rather than an owner. Give proportionally and regularly rather than occasionally and emotionally. Decide in advance what is enough, since a level that is never defined is never reached. And watch the direction of travel: whether your standard of living rises automatically with every increase in income, which is the surest evidence that the heart is set where the treasure is.

The most useful question this chapter puts is Baxter’s own, and it takes about ten seconds to answer. Not how much do you own? — but what could you not bear to lose?

The subtler worldliness

Money is the form of worldliness that gets named, and Baxter thought it was not the most dangerous one for religious people. The subtler form is the love of reputation — the desire to be well thought of, which operates just as powerfully in a congregation as in a marketplace and is almost never confessed, because it disguises itself as a proper concern for one’s testimony. The Lord identified it as an obstacle to faith itself.

How can ye believe, which receive honour one of another, and seek not the honour that cometh from God only? JOHN 5:44

That is a startling sentence. Not it will be difficult but how can ye — the desire for human approval is presented as making faith impossible, because faith requires a valuation of things that the approval-seeker cannot afford to hold. John records the same disease in men who did believe and would not say so.

Nevertheless among the chief rulers also many believed on him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they should be put out of the synagogue: for they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God. JOHN 12:42–43

Baxter’s test for this was to ask what a person is willing to be thought. Would you accept being considered foolish, unsuccessful, unspiritual, or wrong, if faithfulness required it? He noticed that ministers and other religious workers are particularly exposed, since their standing depends on being regarded well by people whose opinion they must also correct — an arrangement almost designed to produce cowardice. The remedy is the same as for money, and it is the cross. A man who has genuinely died has no reputation left to protect.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Answer the question honestly: what could you not bear to lose? That is where your treasure is. 2. Decide what is enough. Write down a figure or a standard, and stop moving it upwards. 3. Check whether your giving has risen in proportion to your income over the last five years. If not, notice what has. 4. Do not try to argue yourself out of the love of money. Spend the time at the cross instead. 5. Give something away this week that you will actually feel.

A PRAYER
Lord, I have called my worldliness prudence and my grasping stewardship, and nobody has ever challenged me because everyone around me does the same.
I know the world is passing. Knowing it has changed nothing.
Break its hold by the only thing strong enough. Show me Your cross until the things I have been clutching lose their shine, and until I am dead to what I have been living for.
Teach me to enjoy Your gifts without setting my heart on them, and to hold them loosely enough to give them away. Amen.

fields.title: Redeeming the Time
fields.body_html:
See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. EPHESIANS 5:15–16

Baxter published around a hundred and forty books. He did it while pastoring a parish of two thousand souls, preaching twice a week, catechising fourteen families a week, carrying on a vast correspondence, engaging in most of the theological controversies of his century — and being seriously ill for practically the whole of it. He was not a well man who worked hard. He was a man in continual pain who expected to die shortly and worked as though he might not finish the sentence.

Time as the material of life

His teaching on time follows directly from his teaching on heaven. If this life is the brief interval in which an eternal condition is settled, then time is not a resource among others. It is the material out of which everything of lasting consequence is made, and it is issued in a quantity nobody knows.

So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. PSALM 90:12
Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away. JAMES 4:14

Baxter’s habitual expectation of an early death was, in one sense, a mistake — he lived to seventy-six. In another sense it was the making of him, because he never once assumed he had time to spare.

Where it actually goes

He was practical about the leaks, and his list has aged remarkably well. Idleness, which he distinguished carefully from rest. Rest is necessary and God-given; idleness is the aimless consumption of hours that produces neither refreshment nor work. Excessive sleep, which he treated as a genuine spiritual issue and about which he was probably harder than he should have been. Unprofitable talk, in which he included most gossip and a good deal of what passes for conversation. Baxter reckoned that many Christians spend more hours a week in idle speech than in all their religious duties combined. Needless recreation. He allowed recreation and thought it necessary, but insisted it be treated as a means — refreshment for work — rather than an end pursued for its own sake. Over-attention to business. Interestingly, he named this too. A man may lose his life to legitimate work as thoroughly as to idleness, and be praised for it throughout.

I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work. JOHN 9:4

How to redeem it

His directions are unremarkable and effective. Know your calling, and give the bulk of your hours to it rather than to whatever presents itself. Plan the day in advance, since unplanned time is almost always lost time. Do the most important thing first, while you are able. Use the fragments — Baxter was a great believer in the odd quarter-hour, and much of his writing was done in intervals. And review at day’s end, which connects this chapter to the last.

Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest. ECCLESIASTES 9:10

An honest qualification

Here Baxter needs correcting, and it would be dishonest not to say so. He drove himself extremely hard, and there is reason to think it cost him. His health was wretched throughout, and while much of that was constitutional, some of it was almost certainly the consequence of a regime no body could sustain. He worked when he should have stopped, and he was severe with himself in ways he would never have been with a parishioner. His teaching can therefore be taken up in a way that damages people, and in an age that already worships productivity the danger is considerable. Two correctives are necessary. Rest is commanded, not merely permitted. God built a day of it into the week and did not make it optional.

Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat. MARK 6:31

That is the Lord’s instruction to workers who were genuinely busy with genuinely important work.

And our worth does not consist in our output. A believer prevented from working by illness, age or circumstance has lost nothing of his standing before God. Baxter, of all people, ought to have known this, and in his better moments he did.

Redeem the time, then — but redeem it for the right things, and remember that sleeping when you are exhausted is one of them.

Ordinary work as service

A necessary balance, since a chapter on time can leave the impression that hours spent on secular work are hours subtracted from God. Baxter held firmly that they are not. His treatment of vocation in A Christian Directory covers trades, farming, commerce and household management at length, and treats them as genuine service rather than as regrettable necessities.

And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men; knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance: for ye serve the Lord Christ. COLOSSIANS 3:23–24

Paul is addressing slaves. If the most degraded labour in the Roman world could be done as service to Christ and receive a reward from Him, then no honest work is outside the arrangement. Baxter drew practical consequences that were unusual in his century and remain useful. Choose a calling, where you have the choice, by its usefulness to others rather than by what it pays. Do it well. Shoddy work by a Christian is a testimony, and not a good one. Treat it as the place where most of your obedience will actually happen. A person converted at twenty and dying at seventy will spend perhaps ninety thousand hours at work and a small fraction of that in explicitly religious activity. If holiness cannot operate in the ninety thousand, it will not amount to much.

Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord. ROMANS 12:11

Baxter put those three together as one instruction, and so did Paul. Diligence at work, warmth of spirit, and service to Christ are not three separate departments of a life.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Track where your hours actually went last week. The gap between your estimate and the truth is the finding. 2. Plan tomorrow tonight. Unplanned time is nearly always lost time. 3. Identify your largest single leak — idleness, talk, screens, or overwork — and address that one rather than everything. 4. Use the fragments. A quarter of an hour, used regularly, adds up to more than most people’s good intentions. 5. Take your rest without guilt. It is commanded, and your worth does not depend on your output.

A PRAYER
Father, You have given me a fixed number of days and I do not know the number.
Teach me to number them. Show me where my hours are going, and give me the resolve to spend them on what will matter when I stand before You.
Deliver me from idleness, and equally from the busyness that looks like faithfulness and is only fear.
And when I need to stop, let me stop without shame — knowing that You value me for what Your Son has done and not for what I produce. Amen.

fields.title: Counsel for the Melancholy
fields.body_html:
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God. PSALM 42:11

Among the most remarkable things Baxter wrote are his treatises on what his century called melancholy — what we would call depression, anxiety and related disorders of the mind. They are remarkable because they are three hundred years ahead of most of what was written on the subject afterwards, and because a great deal of Christian counsel since has been worse.

A disease, not a sin

Baxter’s central insight is that melancholy is frequently a bodily illness that produces spiritual symptoms, and that treating the symptoms as though they were the disease makes everything worse. The natural response of a minister is to address this theologically — to reason with the doubts, urge self-examination, and press the promises. Baxter observed that this frequently fails, and that it fails because the problem is not in the theology. The same person, restored to bodily health, generally finds his doubts have evaporated without a single argument having been answered. The doubts were a product of the condition, not its cause. He therefore insisted that such sufferers need physic as well as spiritual counsel — medical treatment, taken seriously, alongside prayer. In the seventeenth century that was an unusual thing for a divine to say.

What not to do

His directions to counsellors are the most valuable part, and they cut directly against most instincts. Do not press self-examination. This is the great error. A melancholy person turned inward will find fresh evidence against himself indefinitely, because the faculty doing the searching is the one that is disordered. Baxter’s counsel was to turn such people outward — to the promises, to Christ, to other people — and to forbid the introspection that a healthy Christian should be encouraged in.

Do not leave them alone. Solitude and prolonged meditation, which he recommended warmly elsewhere in his writings, he judged actively harmful here. Company, conversation and cheerful occupation do more good. Do not argue with every doubt. The doubts multiply faster than they can be answered, and answering them concedes the premise that the trouble is intellectual. Do not add guilt. Telling a person that their despair is itself a sin, or evidence of weak faith, is both untrue and cruel. Baxter’s counsel needs no correction so much as it needs restating, but two things should be said plainly for a modern reader. If you are suffering in this way, please seek qualified medical help. Depression and anxiety disorders are real illnesses with effective treatments, and consulting a doctor is not a failure of faith any more than it would be for a broken bone. Baxter said as much with the medicine available to him; he would say it far more strongly now. One particular symptom deserves separate treatment, because it distresses sufferers more than almost anything else: the inability to pray. The person finds that prayer has become impossible. Baxter’s counsel here is gentle and entirely practical. Use other people’s words. The Psalms exist for exactly this. A person who cannot construct a prayer can read one, and the Psalter contains a considerable number written by people in this precise condition.

Both are true; only one of them is steady.

You will not break the bruised reed. Be near, as You have promised, to those of a broken heart. Amen.

fields.title: Peace Among Christians
fields.body_html:
Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God. MATTHEW 5:9

Baxter spent his life on this subject and largely failed at it, which makes him an unusually instructive teacher. He laboured for reconciliation between the English religious parties for forty years. He drew up schemes of comprehension, wrote irenic treatises, organised associations across party lines, and served at the Savoy Conference trying to find terms broad enough to keep the moderates together. Almost none of it succeeded in his lifetime. He also quarrelled with practically everyone, at length and in print, and knew it.

Why Christians divide

His analysis of the causes is unsentimental, and it holds up. Pride, which he named first and repeatedly. Most controversy is not really about the question in dispute; it is about being right, being seen to be right, and not being overcome by an opponent.

For ye are yet carnal: for whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal, and walk as men? 1 CORINTHIANS 3:3

Ignorance, in two directions. We do not know enough about the matter in hand, and we do not know enough about our opponent’s actual position — we argue with a version of it we have constructed. Party spirit, which attaches the loyalty due to Christ to a name, a tradition or a leader. Making too many things necessary. Baxter’s chief structural point: divisions multiply in proportion to the length of the list of things everyone must agree on. Shorten the list and much of the conflict disappears.

Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations. ROMANS 14:1

How to conduct a disagreement

He gave practical directions, and they are usable in a church committee this month.

State your opponent’s view in terms he would accept before you answer it. Baxter regarded failure here as evidence of bad faith or laziness, and most controversy as therefore illegitimate before it starts. Distinguish the person from the position, and the position from its worst consequences. A man is not responsible for conclusions he does not draw. Ask whether the matter is worth the cost. Baxter’s rule was that the damage done by pressing a point must be weighed against the good of settling it, and that many battles are lost by winning them. Allow that a godly man may hold what you consider mistaken. This was his strongest theme in later life — that the differences among genuinely converted people are smaller than the difference between the converted and the unconverted, and that we habitually get the proportions backwards.

But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy. JAMES 3:17

Note the order. Pure first — peace is not bought by abandoning truth — and then peaceable, gentle, and willing to be persuaded.

The limits of peace

Baxter was not advocating peace at any price, and his own life proves it. He was ejected from the church he loved rather than subscribe to terms he judged false, and he went to prison rather than be silent.

If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men. ROMANS 12:18

Paul’s two qualifications are the whole doctrine. If it be possible — sometimes it is not, and the fault may be entirely on the other side. As much as lieth in you — our responsibility extends to our own conduct and no further. A Christian is not obliged to secure peace; he is obliged not to be the one who breaks it.

The man himself

Now the honest part, and Baxter would have wanted it said. The greatest English writer on Christian peace was, by temperament, a controversialist. He could not leave an argument alone. He answered every attack, usually at length. He wrote so much polemic that his friends begged him to stop, and his own admission late in life was that he had written too much, too fast, and too sharply. There is something instructive in the gap. It suggests that a man may see a duty clearly, teach it well, and struggle with it all his days — and that his teaching is not thereby invalidated. Baxter knew what peace required precisely because he had spent so long failing to achieve it. He also, and this is the redeeming part, kept changing. The self-assessment in his autobiography records a man who had grown steadily gentler, less certain of his own judgment, and more willing to think well of those who differed. He was still arguing at the end. He was arguing differently.

The test of this chapter is not whether you value unity. It is what you do in the next disagreement. Specifically: can you state the other person’s view in terms they would accept? If not, you are not yet in a position to answer it.

The Worcestershire experiment

Baxter’s most successful contribution to Christian unity was not a book or a scheme of comprehension. It was a local association of ministers, and its story is instructive. In the early 1650s he gathered the ministers of Worcestershire — Presbyterians, Independents and men of episcopalian conviction — into a voluntary association. They agreed to co-operate in three practical things: the discipline of their congregations, the systematic catechising of their parishes, and mutual counsel. What they did not do was resolve their differences. The question of church government, over which the nation was tearing itself apart, was deliberately left open. They simply agreed to work together on what they could agree about. It succeeded. Other counties copied the model, and for a few years there existed in parts of England a working co-operation between parties that were at war everywhere else.

Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity! PSALM 133:1

Two lessons come out of it. The first is that unity is more achievable locally than nationally. Baxter’s grand schemes at the Savoy Conference failed completely; his county association worked. Men who know each other, whose congregations overlap, and who face the same practical problems can cooperate on a basis that abstract negotiation never reaches. The second is that shared work unites better than shared agreement. The Worcestershire ministers did not become friends by settling their disputes. They became friends by catechising the same county, and the disputes mattered less afterwards.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. In your next disagreement, state the other position in terms its holder would accept before you reply. If you cannot, you do not yet understand it. 2. Ask of your current controversy whether the good of winning outweighs the damage of fighting. Some battles are lost by winning them. 3. Shorten your list. How many things must someone agree with you on before you can regard them as a brother? 4. Distinguish the person from the position, and the position from consequences they do not draw. 5. Where peace has failed, check whether the failure lies with you. That is the only part you are answerable for.

A PRAYER
Lord, I have argued for truth and enjoyed the arguing, and I have not always been able to tell the difference.
Show me where my convictions are really about being right. Give me the honesty to state fairly what those who differ from me actually believe.
Make me peaceable without making me hollow — pure first, and then gentle, and willing to be persuaded.
And where peace is not possible, let the fault never be mine. Amen.

fields.title: Suffering and Patience
fields.body_html:
Our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:17

Baxter is worth hearing on this subject because he had unusual qualifications. He was ill from his early twenties until his death at seventy-six, in continual pain, with a catalogue of complaints he recorded with a physician’s precision. He was expelled at forty-six from the parish he had given his life to, and forbidden ever to return. He was harassed for a quarter of a century, fined, and had his goods and books seized. He buried the wife he loved. He was imprisoned at seventy, after a trial in which the Lord Chief Justice abused him from the bench and would not let his counsel speak. He wrote about affliction as a man reporting on a country he lived in.

What suffering is for

He refused two explanations that were common then and are common now. He would not say that suffering is meaningless — an accident in a world God does not govern. And he would not say that it is always punishment for particular sins, which is the error of Job’s friends and which he had watched destroy people. His position was that God uses affliction purposefully, and that its purposes are several.

And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope. ROMANS 5:3–4

It weans us from the world, which no amount of preaching accomplishes. It exposes what is actually in us, which prosperity conceals. It teaches dependence. It fits a man to comfort others, since no one is much use to the suffering who has not suffered.

Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God. 2 CORINTHIANS 1:4

Patience is not passivity

Baxter distinguished patience carefully from resignation, apathy and stoicism. Christian patience is not the suppression of feeling. Scripture’s sufferers complain loudly — the Psalms are full of it, Job says what he thinks, and the Lord Himself asked in Gethsemane for the cup to be removed. Baxter had no patience with a piety that required people to pretend they were untroubled. What patience means is continuing to trust and obey while the trouble lasts. It is a matter of direction rather than of temperature.

Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him. JOB 13:15

He added a practical observation. Most people can bear a great deal if they know it will end. What breaks us is indefiniteness — not knowing how long. And this, he said, is precisely where the doctrine of heaven does its work, because it supplies the one certainty that matters: there is a term, and what lies past it is out of all proportion to what precedes it.

The arithmetic

Paul’s comparison in 2 Corinthians 4 is the passage Baxter returned to most, and he insisted it be read as a sober calculation rather than a pious flourish. Light affliction — from a man who had been flogged five times, stoned, shipwrecked and imprisoned. For a moment — from a man who had endured it for decades. The words are not a denial of the weight; they are a comparison, and the other term of the comparison is an eternal weight of glory. Baxter’s point was that the arithmetic works only if you can see both figures. Which brings the matter back to chapter eleven: what we call impatience is usually a failure of sight.

For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us. ROMANS 8:18

When it does not feel like this

An honest note, because chapters on suffering can be written by people who have not suffered and read by people who are. Baxter did not always manage this. His writings from the worst periods contain plenty of distress, complaint and something close to despair. He lost his temper with God, and said so. That should be a relief rather than a disappointment. The doctrine does not require you to feel it working. A believer flat on his back, unable to pray, unable to see any purpose, and merely enduring, is not failing — he is suffering, which is what the doctrine is about.

Nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby. HEBREWS 12:11

Afterward. The fruit is not visible during. That is stated in the text, and it is worth remembering when nothing appears to be happening.

Baxter kept his post for fifty years under conditions that would have justified retirement several times over, and produced most of his work while expecting to die. He was not made of different material. He simply kept going, which is generally what patience turns out to consist of.

Before Judge Jeffreys

Baxter’s teaching on patience can be tested against a documented occasion, which is more than most writers on the subject can offer. In May 1685 he was seventy years old, in poor health, and charged with sedition for supposed reflections on the bishops in his Paraphrase on the New Testament. He was tried before Lord Chief Justice Jeffreys, whose conduct on the bench is one of the more notorious episodes in English legal history. Jeffreys abused him throughout. He called him an old rogue who had poisoned the world with his Kidderminster doctrine, mocked his appearance, refused to let his counsel present the defence, and at one point suggested he deserved to be whipped through the city. Baxter’s recorded conduct was to remain quiet, to answer briefly when permitted, and at one point to remark that he was not concerned to answer such language. He was convicted, fined a sum he could not pay, and imprisoned for some twenty-one months.

fields.body_html:
For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better. PHILIPPIANS 1:23

In 1683, at sixty-seven, widowed and infirm, Baxter published a book of meditations on Paul’s words about departing to be with Christ. He called it Dying Thoughts, and he wrote it, as he had written The Saints’ Everlasting Rest thirty-six years earlier, for himself. The two books frame his life. He wrote the first at thirty-one expecting to die within months, and the second at sixty-seven, still expecting it, and by then with rather better grounds.

Preparing before it arrives

His central practical argument is that dying well is a matter of preparation, and that preparation cannot begin when the event does. A man who has spent fifty years avoiding the subject will not acquire, in his last fortnight, a settled mind about it. The habits of thought that carry a person through will have been formed decades before, in health, when nothing was pressing.

So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. PSALM 90:12

Baxter recommended the deliberate contemplation of one’s own death, at intervals, as a Christian discipline — not morbidly, and not as a way of frightening oneself, but as the only realistic way of getting one’s affairs, priorities and affections into proportion.

It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart. ECCLESIASTES 7:2

Why it is far better

Paul’s phrase carried the weight of the book, and Baxter took it apart. Far better — not merely tolerable, not merely a release. Better than the best of what we have here, including the things we most love. He set out why, and it is a summary of everything in this book. Because sin will end. Because the struggle will end. Because we shall see Christ, whom we have loved without seeing. Because we shall understand what we have spent our lives failing to understand. Because the church will be gathered and undivided — a point Baxter felt with unusual sharpness, having spent forty years watching it tear itself apart.

For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:1

Fear, honestly treated

Baxter did not pretend that believers face death without fear, and he was notably gentle here. He distinguished the natural shrinking of the body from the fear of God’s wrath. The first is instinctive and is no more sinful than flinching from fire; the Lord Himself sweated in a garden. The second is dealt with, and if a believer is still labouring under it, the remedy is not more resolve but a clearer sight of what Christ has done.

O death, where is thy sting? …The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. 1 CORINTHIANS 15:55–57

He added counsel for those attending the dying: not to press them with examination at the end, not to demand expressions of assurance from people too weak to produce them, and to speak the promises rather than ask questions. A person’s safety at that hour does not rest on the state of their feelings, and it is cruel to make them think it does.

How it ended

Baxter died on the eighth of December, 1691, at seventy-six, in London. He had been in pain most of his life and considerable pain at the end. He had outlived his wife by ten years, the parish he loved by nearly thirty, and most of the causes he had fought for. He had seen the Toleration Act pass two years earlier, which was the nearest thing to a victory he ever had. Those with him reported that when asked how he was, he answered that he was almost well. It is a small joke and a whole theology. He had spent fifty years telling people that this life is the sickness and the next is the recovery, and at the end he was still saying it, from the bed, to whoever asked.

I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness. 2 TIMOTHY 4:7–8

He is one of the few writers who can be trusted entirely on this subject, because he never wrote a line about heaven that he was not shortly expecting to test.

And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord. REVELATION 14:13

There remains a rest for the people of God, and Richard Baxter went into it, having written about it for forty-four years longer than he thought he would.

Those who have gone before

There is a dimension of the Christian’s hope that Baxter felt with particular force after 1681, when Margaret died and he was left alone for the last decade of his life. The New Testament describes the church as one body which death does not divide. The believers who have died are not gone; they are elsewhere, and we are told where.

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight …and let us run with patience the race that is set before us. HEBREWS 12:1
To the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect. HEBREWS 12:23

Baxter took considerable comfort from the thought that the company he was going to already contained people he knew — his wife, his friends, the parishioners he had buried at Kidderminster, and the writers whose books had converted and formed him and whom he had never met. He was careful about the limits. Scripture does not encourage us to address the dead or to imagine we can communicate with them, and he had no patience with speculation of that kind. What it does teach is that they are alive, that they are with Christ, and that the separation is temporary.

For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him …Wherefore comfort one another with these words. 1 THESSALONIANS 4:14, 18

For the bereaved reader, that is the entire point of the doctrine, and Paul says so in as many words. It is given to be used.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Think deliberately about your own death this week — not morbidly, but long enough to see what it does to your priorities.

2. Put your affairs in order: the will, the debts, the letter you have been meaning to write, the reconciliation you have postponed. 3. Distinguish natural fear from the fear of wrath. The first is human; the second has been dealt with. 4. If you sit with the dying, speak the promises rather than asking questions. Do not require assurance from those too weak to produce it. 5. Ask what you would want to be doing at the end, and do more of it now.

A PRAYER
Lord, I have arranged my life as though it would not end, and I will not have the sense to prepare at the last minute if I have not begun now.
Teach me to number my days. Let the thought of standing before You sort out what matters from what does not, while there is still time to act on it.
Take away the sting. Whatever natural fear remains, let me not fear Your wrath, for Your Son has borne it.
And when the hour comes, let me be found where Your servant was — almost well, and nearly home. Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord. 1 CORINTHIANS 15:58

Eighteen chapters can suggest that Richard Baxter taught a great many things. In one sense he did — he wrote around a hundred and forty books and had opinions on everything. But the working principle underneath is single, and it is stated in the verse above. It is this: eternity is real; therefore work. That is the whole man. The two halves of his reputation — the theologian of heaven and the model of pastoral diligence — are not two interests that happened to coexist in one person. They are cause and effect. He catechised illiterate weavers two days a week because he believed each of them would exist for ever. He wrote about the saints’ rest and then behaved as though there were no time to rest at all, and there is no contradiction in that whatever. Take away the eternity and the labour becomes fanaticism. Take away the labour and the eternity becomes sentiment. Baxter held them together, and everything else in this book follows: the urgency of his evangelism, the weight he placed on personal instruction, the seriousness about time, the household as a mission field, the refusal to divide over secondary things when the primary thing was so enormous.

The danger of this book

If you have read this far, there is a particular hazard, and it is the opposite of the one attending the other volumes in this series. Baxter is exhausting. His standard is extremely high, his tone is urgent, and he was capable of a diligence that almost nobody can match — and did not always recognise that. A conscientious reader can finish him convinced that he has never done anything properly in his life, and be paralysed rather than moved. That would be a misuse. Baxter wrote to rouse the complacent, not to crush the willing, and his own theology gives the corrective. A believer’s acceptance rests on Christ and not on his productivity. The man who spent his life urging others to labour finished his own by observing, from bed, that he was almost well — not that he had done enough.

For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust. PSALM 103:14

So take one thing. Not the whole programme — one thing. Fix a family worship time, or begin meeting with one person, or set twenty minutes for meditation on what is coming. Baxter’s method was never grandeur; it was a modest practice sustained for years.

Two things to carry

First, the eternal weight of ordinary people. If Baxter has one gift for the modern church it is this. He looked at a weaving town of two thousand unimpressive people and saw two thousand immortal souls, and it reorganised his diary. That vision, more than any technique, is what produced the ministry everyone has admired ever since. Second, the shortness of the list. Baxter spent forty years arguing and concluded that the things necessary to be believed are fewer and plainer than controversialists suppose, that the difference between godly Christians is smaller than we think, and that the difference between the godly and the ungodly is larger. Every generation needs to hear it and none has ever much wanted to.

A last word about the man

We have been honest about his failures. His doctrine of justification was judged by most of his own tradition to compromise the freeness of the gospel, and chapter six sets out why the objection has force. He was contentious, and the greatest English writer on Christian peace quarrelled with almost everybody. He wrote far too much and admitted it. He drove a sick body past what it could bear and called it faithfulness. His political judgment was, by his own account, repeatedly wrong. None of that is raised to diminish him. It is raised because he raised it about himself, at length, in an autobiography which contains one of the most honest pieces of self-assessment in the language — a man in old age listing the ways his mind had changed, and finding himself less certain, less impressed by cleverness, and slower to condemn than he had been at thirty. That is worth more than most people’s virtues. A teacher who has learned something from his own mistakes is more useful than one who never made any.

But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:7

Kidderminster remembered him for generations. The manual he dashed off for a county association of ministers is still set for theological students three and a half centuries later. The book he wrote on what he assumed was his deathbed at thirty-one has been consoling the dying ever since. He expected none of it. He expected to be dead by the spring.

A PRAYER
Lord, I believe in eternity and it has changed almost nothing about my week.
Give me Baxter’s sight — to look at the ordinary people around me and see souls that will outlast the stars, and to let that reorder what I do with my hours.
Keep me from being crushed by what I cannot do. Let me take one thing and be faithful in it for years.
And shorten my list. Let me hold the great things firmly, the small things loosely, and every brother charitably.
I am almost well, and nearly home. Keep me at my post until then. Amen.

Give me Baxter’s sight — to look at the ordinary people around me and see souls that will outlast the stars, and to let that reorder what I do with my hours. Keep me from being crushed by what I cannot do. Let me take one thing and be faithful in it for years. And shorten my list. Let me hold the great things firmly, the small things loosely, and every brother charitably. I am almost well, and nearly home. Keep me at my post until then. Amen.

fields.title: A Reader’s Guide to Richard Baxter
fields.body_html:
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth. 2 TIMOTHY 2:15

Baxter presents the reader with two difficulties: there is far too much of him, and his prose is heavy going. He published around a hundred and forty works. His sentences are long even by seventeenth-century standards, he qualifies everything, and he never uses one clause where four will serve. His friends complained about it in his lifetime. The good news is that everything is in the public domain, that several of his best works exist in excellent modern abridgements, and that the abridgements are the right place to start. There is no virtue in struggling through an unabridged folio when a competent editor has already done the work.

Begin here

The Reformed Pastor (1656). His most useful book and the one still read. Modern abridged editions run to a couple of hundred pages and lose nothing essential. Every pastor, elder and Sunday school teacher should read it once, with the caution of chapter seven in mind. A Call to the Unconverted (1658). Short, plain, and written for people with little education. Still usable as an evangelistic gift. The Saints’ Everlasting Rest (1650), in abridgement. The full work runs to four substantial parts; the abridgements generally preserve the description of heaven and the directions for heavenly contemplation, which are what most readers want.

On the Christian life

Dying Thoughts (1683). Meditations on Philippians 1:23, written in old age. Short and moving. The Life of Faith. The basis of chapter eleven; on living by the unseen. The Poor Man’s Family Book. Written for households with little education, in dialogue form. A window into how he actually taught. A Breviate of the Life of Margaret Baxter (1681). His memoir of his wife, written within weeks of her death. Not theology, and one of the most affecting things in the century — a widower’s portrait of a woman he plainly thought his better.

The great practical work

A Christian Directory (1673). An enormous manual of practical theology and cases of conscience, running to something like a million words, covering private devotion, family life, church relations and public dealings. Not to be read through. It is a reference work, and it is worth consulting on any question of Christian practice you can think of, because he almost certainly addressed it.

On melancholy

Baxter’s writings on melancholy and overmuch sorrow, discussed in chapter fifteen, are scattered and less easy to obtain, but worth seeking out. They are three centuries ahead of most of what followed and remain among the wisest Christian counsel on the subject. Read them with the modern note supplied in that chapter: seek qualified medical help.

Approach with care

Aphorisms of Justification (1649) and the long train of controversial writings that followed it. This is the material discussed in chapter six. Read it only if you want to understand the debate, and read the objections alongside it. The polemical works more generally. There are a great many, they are exhausting, and Baxter himself came to regret their number and their sharpness.

His own account

Reliquiae Baxterianae, his autobiography, published in 1696 after his death. The full text is unwieldy; the standard abridgement is far more readable and contains the famous passage on how his mind changed with age, which is the single best thing he wrote about himself.

About Baxter

Geoffrey Nuttall’s Richard Baxter (1965) is a compact and reliable scholarly life. J. I. Packer wrote his doctoral work on Baxter’s theology and returned to him repeatedly afterwards; the chapters on Baxter in A Quest for Godliness are the best short appreciation available, and are candid about the justification problem. N. H. Keeble has written well on Baxter as a writer and on the Nonconformist world he inhabited. Read more than one. Baxter attracts admirers who overlook his faults and critics who overlook everything else.

Three counsels for reading him

Read the abridgements first, and without embarrassment. The editors have removed repetition, not substance. Read him for the burden rather than the system. Where he presses beyond Scripture — and on justification he does — take the pastoral concern and leave the framework. And read him in small quantities. Baxter is rich and heavy, and a few pages digested will do more than fifty pages endured. He would have said the same; he said it about his own writing more than once.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21
